Abstract.

This work investigates the global existence, uniqueness, and Feller property for stochastic partial differential equations under generalized coercivity conditions, particularly in cases where the corresponding deterministic equations possess only local solutions. Furthermore, we reveal a novel phenomenon: for a potentially explosive deterministic system, the introduction of appropriate multiplicative noise not only prevents blow-up but also leads to the finite-time extinction of the stochastic dynamics. Our main results are applicable to a broad range of models, including stochastic 3D Navier-Stokes equations, stochastic surface growth models, and stochastic pp-Laplace equations with heat sources.

Keywords: Stochastic PDEs; Generalized coercivity; Well-posedness; Feller property; Finite-time extinction.
Mathematics Subject Classification (2020): 60H15, 35R60

1. Introduction

This work focuses on stochastic partial differential equations (SPDEs) within the variational framework. Originating from the pioneering work of Minty [45], the variational approach was subsequently and systematically developed by Browder [9, 10], Leray and Lions [36], and Hartman and Stampacchia [24].

We begin by reviewing the fundamental concepts of the variational approach and summarizing relevant developments in the literature. Let (U,⟨⋅,⋅⟩U)(U,\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_{U}) and (ℍ,⟨⋅,⋅⟩ℍ)({\mathbb{H}},\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_{\mathbb{H}}) be separable Hilbert spaces, and ℍ∗{\mathbb{H}}^{*} be the dual space of ℍ{\mathbb{H}}. Let (𝕍,∥⋅∥𝕍)({\mathbb{V}},\|\cdot\|_{\mathbb{V}}) denote a reflexive Banach space such that the embedding

𝕍⊂ℍ\mathbb{V}\subset\mathbb{H}

is continuous and dense. Identifying ℍ\mathbb{H} with its dual space in view of the Riesz isomorphism, we obtain a Gelfand triple

(1.1) 𝕍⊂ℍ(≃ℍ∗)⊂𝕍∗.{\mathbb{V}}\subset{\mathbb{H}}(\simeq{\mathbb{H}}^{*})\subset{\mathbb{V}}^{*}.

The dualization between 𝕍{\mathbb{V}} and 𝕍∗{\mathbb{V}}^{*} is denoted by ⟨⋅,⋅⟩𝕍𝕍∗{}_{{\mathbb{V}}^{*}}\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_{\mathbb{V}}. It is clear that

⟨⋅,⋅⟩𝕍𝕍∗|ℍ×𝕍=⟨⋅,⋅⟩ℍ.{}_{{\mathbb{V}}^{*}}\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_{\mathbb{V}}|_{{\mathbb{H}}\times{\mathbb{V}}}=\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_{\mathbb{H}}.

Let L2​(U,ℍ)L_{2}(U,\mathbb{H}) be the space of all Hilbert-Schmidt operators from UU to ℍ\mathbb{H}. For measurable maps

𝒜:[0,T]×𝕍→𝕍∗,ℬ:[0,T]×𝕍→L2​(U,ℍ),\mathcal{A}:[0,T]\times{\mathbb{V}}\rightarrow{\mathbb{V}}^{*},\penalty\ \penalty\ \mathcal{B}:[0,T]\times{\mathbb{V}}\rightarrow L_{2}(U,\mathbb{H}),

we consider the following SPDE

(1.2) d​Xt=𝒜⁡(t,Xt)​d​t+ℬ⁡(t,Xt)​d​Wt,X0=x,dX_{t}=\mathcal{A}(t,X_{t})dt+\mathcal{B}(t,X_{t})dW_{t},\penalty\ \penalty\ X_{0}=x,

where {Wt}t∈[0,T]\{W_{t}\}_{t\in[0,T]} is an UU-valued cylindrical Wiener process defined on a complete filtered probability space (Ω,ℱ,{ℱt}t∈[0,T],ℙ)\left(\Omega,\mathscr{F},\{\mathscr{F}_{t}\}_{t\in[0,T]},\mathbb{P}\right).

In the deterministic case (i.e., ℬ≡0\mathcal{B}\equiv 0), the classical result states that Eq. (1.2) has a unique solution if the operator 𝒜\mathcal{A} satisfies the monotonicity condition

(1.3) ⟨𝒜(t,u)−𝒜(t,v),u−v⟩𝕍𝕍∗≤C∥u−v∥ℍ2{}_{\mathbb{V}^{*}}\langle\mathcal{A}(t,u)-\mathcal{A}(t,v),u-v\rangle_{\mathbb{V}}\leq C\|u-v\|_{\mathbb{H}}^{2}

and the coercivity condition (see e.g. [71, Thoerem 30.A])

(1.4) ⟨𝒜(t,u),u⟩𝕍𝕍∗+δ∥u∥𝕍α≤C∥u∥ℍ2+C,{}_{\mathbb{V}^{*}}\langle\mathcal{A}(t,u),u\rangle_{\mathbb{V}}+\delta\|u\|_{\mathbb{V}}^{\alpha}\leq C\|u\|_{\mathbb{H}}^{2}+C,

where δ,C>0\delta,C>0 and α>1\alpha>1.

In the stochastic setting, the variational approach was initiated by Pardoux [50] and Krylov and Rozovskii [33] for SPDEs with coefficients satisfying the monotonicity (1.3) and coercivity (1.4) conditions. These classical results apply to a class of quasi-linear stochastic models, such as the stochastic porous medium equation and the stochastic pp-Laplace equation (see, e.g., [52, 54]).

It is important to note that the previous works, both in deterministic and stochastic cases, require that the operator 𝒜\mathcal{A} satisfies the classical coercivity condition (1.4), which ensures global-in-time bounds of solutions. In this work, we are interested in SPDEs satisfying the following generalized coercivity condition

(1.5) 2𝕍∗​⟨𝒜⁡(t,u),u⟩𝕍+δ​‖u‖𝕍α≤g⁡(‖u‖ℍ2)+C,\displaystyle 2_{\mathbb{V}^{*}}\langle\mathcal{A}(t,u),u\rangle_{\mathbb{V}}+\delta\|u\|_{\mathbb{V}}^{\alpha}\leq g(\|u\|_{\mathbb{H}}^{2})+C,

where δ,C>0\delta,C>0 and g:[0,∞)→[0,∞)g:[0,\infty)\to[0,\infty) is a non-decreasing continuous function. This condition was considered by Liu and Röckner in [42, Section 5.2] (see also [41]). Many important models satisfy the condition (1.5), yet fail to satisfy the classical coercivity condition (1.4). Typical models that fit into this framework include

  • •

    3D Navier–Stokes equations:

    {∂tu=νΔu−(u⋅∇)u−∇p+f,div​(u)=0.\displaystyle\left\{\begin{aligned} &\partial_{t}{u}=\nu\Delta{u}-(u\cdot{\nabla})u-\nabla{p}+f,\\ &\text{div}(u)=0.\end{aligned}\right.
  • •

    Surface growth models:

    ∂tu=−∂x4u−∂x2u+∂x2(∂xu)2.\partial_{t}{u}=-\partial_{x}^{4}u-\partial_{x}^{2}u+\partial_{x}^{2}(\partial_{x}u)^{2}.
  • •

    pp-Laplace equations with heat sources:

    ∂tu=div(|∇u|p−2∇u)+u2.\partial_{t}{u}=\text{div}(|\nabla u|^{p-2}\nabla u)+u^{2}.

Under this assumption, they proved the existence and uniqueness of local solutions to SPDEs (1.2) perturbed by additive noise (i.e., ℬ⁡(t,u)=ℬ⁡(t)\mathcal{B}(t,u)=\mathcal{B}(t)). However, the global well-posedness of SPDEs under this generalized coercivity condition has not yet been established.

1.1. Well-posedness

The first aim of this paper is to establish the well-posedness of SPDEs satisfying the generalized coercivity condition (1.5). Before presenting our main results, we first review the research progress achieved within the variational framework in the literature. In [40], Liu and Röckner extended the classical variational framework by introducing the following local monotonicity condition

(1.6) ⟨𝒜(t,u)−𝒜(t,v),u−v⟩𝕍𝕍∗≤(C+ρ(v))∥u−v∥ℍ2,{}_{\mathbb{V}^{*}}\langle\mathcal{A}(t,u)-\mathcal{A}(t,v),u-v\rangle_{\mathbb{V}}\leq(C+\rho(v))\|u-v\|_{\mathbb{H}}^{2},

where ρ:𝕍→[0,+∞)\rho:\mathbb{V}\rightarrow[0,+\infty) is a measurable function that is locally bounded on 𝕍\mathbb{V}. This extension includes various examples that cannot be treated previously, such as stochastic Burgers equations and stochastic 2D Navier-Stokes equations.

More recently, several notable advancements have been made in this direction. Agresti and Veraar [1] introduced a critical variational framework for SPDEs under local Lipschitz conditions, greatly generalizing the classical setup. By employing pseudo-monotone operators and compactness arguments, Shang et al. [57] further generalized the variational framework to a fully local monotonicity condition

(1.7) ⟨𝒜(t,u)−𝒜(t,v),u−v⟩𝕍𝕍∗≤(C+ρ(v)+η(u))∥u−v∥ℍ2,{}_{\mathbb{V}^{*}}\langle\mathcal{A}(t,u)-\mathcal{A}(t,v),u-v\rangle_{\mathbb{V}}\leq(C+\rho(v)+\eta(u))\|u-v\|_{\mathbb{H}}^{2},

where ρ\rho and η\eta are measurable and locally bounded on 𝕍\mathbb{V}. The results in [1] and [57] can be applied to several new models, including the 3D tamed Navier-Stokes equations and Cahn-Hilliard equations. For further developments on the variational framework, we refer the interested reader to [23, 26, 27, 28, 43, 46, 66, 67] and the references therein.

In the present paper, we study global solutions of SPDEs whose coefficients satisfy the generalized coercivity condition (1.5) and fully local monotonicity condition (1.7) under suitable stochastic perturbations. More precisely, we consider diffusion coefficients in the random noise satisfying

(1.8) g⁡(‖u‖ℍ2)+‖ℬ⁡(t,u)‖L2​(U,ℍ)2≤C⁡(1+‖u‖ℍ2)+η0​‖ℬ​(t,u)∗​u‖U2(1+‖u‖ℍ2),g(\|u\|_{\mathbb{H}}^{2})+\|\mathcal{B}(t,u)\|_{L_{2}({U},{\mathbb{H}})}^{2}\leq C(1+\|u\|_{\mathbb{H}}^{2})+\eta_{0}\frac{\|\mathcal{B}(t,u)^{*}u\|_{U}^{2}}{(1+\|u\|_{\mathbb{H}}^{2})},

where η0∈(1,2)\eta_{0}\in(1,2), C>0C>0, and gg is the same function as in (1.5). This condition reflects an anisotropic stabilizing mechanism: only the component of the noise acting along the energy direction contributes to the prevention of blow-up.

Our first main results concern the global well-posedness and the Feller property of SPDEs under the fully local monotonicity condition (1.7) and the generalized coercivity condition (1.5) and (1.8). A more precise statement of these results is provided in Theorems 2.4 and 2.5.

Theorem 1.1.

Suppose that the embedding 𝕍⊂ℍ\mathbb{V}\subset\mathbb{H} is compact and that assumptions (𝐀𝟏)(\mathbf{A_{1}})-(𝐀𝟓)(\mathbf{A_{5}}) (see Subsection 2.1 below) hold.

  1. (i)

    For any initial data x∈ℍx\in\mathbb{H}, Eq. (1.2) has a unique strong solution XtX_{t}. Moreover, the following energy moment estimates hold

    (1.9) supt∈[0,T]𝔼​‖Xt‖ℍ2−η0+𝔼​∫0T‖Xt‖𝕍α−η0​𝑑t<∞.\sup_{t\in[0,T]}\mathbb{E}\|X_{t}\|_{\mathbb{H}}^{2-\eta_{0}}+\mathbb{E}\int_{0}^{T}\|X_{t}\|_{\mathbb{V}}^{\alpha-\eta_{0}}dt<\infty.
  2. (ii)

    The solution depends continuously on the initial values. In particular, the corresponding Markov semigroup (𝒯t)t≥0(\mathcal{T}_{t})_{t\geq 0} possesses the Feller property.

We make several remarks regarding the above results.

  • •

    Note that under the generalized coercivity condition (1.5), the corresponding deterministic PDE (i.e., when the noise term vanishes) may exhibit finite-time blow-up. Consequently, compared with existing literature, the key feature of our work lies in capturing the effect of random noise, which, to the best of our knowledge, is the first such result within the variational framework.

  • •

    To establish the global existence of solutions, it is essential to balance the influence of the noise intensity against the growth rate of the nonlinear terms. In this regard, condition (1.8) plays a crucial role. Roughly speaking, when g⁡(x)=C0​xg(x)=C_{0}x, which corresponds to the classical coercivity condition (1.4), the diffusion term can either vanish or take the form of additive, linear, or superlinear multiplicative noise. In contrast, if g⁡(x)=C0​xpg(x)=C_{0}x^{p} with p>1p>1, then ℬ⁡(t,⋅)\mathcal{B}(t,\cdot) is required to exhibit superlinear growth.

  • •

    From the energy estimate (1.9), one observes that, unlike existing results in the variational framework (see, e.g., [40, 57]), finite second moments are not available for the global solutions. This limitation is inherent to the Lyapunov approach utilized to characterize the influence of stochastic perturbations.

Our new framework establishes general conditions that guarantee global existence and uniqueness. We demonstrate that various classical SPDEs, which lie outside the scope of the standard variational framework, indeed satisfy the generalized coercivity condition (1.5). In particular, our results apply to stochastic pp-Laplace equations with heat sources. Furthermore, our main theorems can be applied to a broad class of stochastic models arising in fluid dynamics, such as the stochastic 3D Navier–Stokes equations and the stochastic surface growth models; these models cannot be accommodated by existing works [1, 40, 46, 57]. Notably, the global well-posedness of the deterministic 3D Navier–Stokes equations remains a long-standing open problem.

Moreover, all locally or fully locally monotone examples studied in [40] and [57], such as stochastic porous medium equations, stochastic 2D Navier–Stokes equations, stochastic Cahn–Hilliard equations, stochastic liquid crystal models, and stochastic Allen–Cahn–Navier–Stokes systems, can be accommodated within the more general framework established in this paper. Furthermore, for these models, our results can be applied to handle random noises with both linear and superlinear growth.

1.2. Finite-time extinction

Building on the global well-posedness result, we investigate the asymptotic behavior of Eq. (1.2) in this setting. In particular, a natural question concerns the influence of noise on the long-time dynamics of stochastic systems. Here, we mainly focus on whether suitable stochastic perturbations can prevent or promote finite-time extinction of solutions.

The phenomenon of finite-time extinction is generally divided into the following three cases

  1. (i)

    Local weak extinction: For small initial values, we have

    ℙ⁡(Xt​extinct in finite time)>0;\mathbb{P}(X_{t}\penalty\ \text{extinct in finite time})>0;
  2. (ii)

    Global weak extinction: For all initial values, we have

    ℙ⁡(Xt​extinct in finite time)>0;\mathbb{P}(X_{t}\penalty\ \text{extinct in finite time})>0;
  3. (iii)

    Almost sure global extinction: For all initial values, we have

    ℙ⁡(Xt​extinct in finite time)=1.\mathbb{P}(X_{t}\penalty\ \text{extinct in finite time})=1.

While Regimes (i) and (ii) are mathematically intriguing, the robustness of the relaxation into subcritical states in self-organized criticality (SOC) is of fundamental importance in physics. Consequently, Regime (iii) aligns most closely with the paradigm of SOC.

There have been many studies in the literature on the finite-time extinction of stochastic systems. For example, Barbu, Da Prato and Röckner [5] investigated the finite-time extinction with positive probability for 1D stochastic SOC models driven by linear multiplicative noise. In a subsequent work [7], Barbu and Röckner established asymptotic extinction results with probability one for stochastic porous media equations in dimension d∈{1,2,3}d\in\{1,2,3\}. This result was further extended by Röckner and Wang [58] to more general cases. Specifically, they proved the finite-time extinction with probability one for the Zhang model, and with positive probability for the Bak-Tang-Wiesenfeld (BTW) model. Notably, the finite-time extinction of the BTW model with probability one remained an open problem until it was resolved by Gess [19] for all dimensions d≥1d\geq 1. For more results of this topic, we refer interested readers to [6, 8, 25] and references therein.

It is worth noting that existing results on finite-time extinction relies on the structure of linear multiplicative noise. In contrast, our work establishes almost sure extinction for any initial value x∈ℍx\in\mathbb{H} (i.e. Case (iii)) for a large class of quasi-linear SPDEs driven by linear or nonlinear multiplicative noises. This leads to the following main result (for details, see Theorem 2.6 below).

Theorem 1.2.

Let τe\tau_{e} denote the extinction time. Under the assumptions of Theorem 1.1, together with the additional conditions (𝐀𝟑∗)(\mathbf{A_{3}^{*}}) and (𝐀𝟓∗)(\mathbf{A_{5}^{*}}) (see Section 2.2 for details), for any initial value x∈ℍx\in\mathbb{H}, the solution XtX_{t} of Eq. (1.2) is extinct in finite time almost surely. Furthermore, the extinction time satisfies the estimates

ℙ⁡(τe>T)≤c0​‖x‖ℍ2−αT\mathbb{P}(\tau_{e}>T)\leq\frac{c_{0}\|x\|_{\mathbb{H}}^{2-\alpha}}{T}

and

𝔼​τe≤c0​‖x‖ℍ2−α,\mathbb{E}\tau_{e}\leq c_{0}\|x\|_{\mathbb{H}}^{2-\alpha},

where c0c_{0} is an explicit constant.

As an application of our general results, we consider the following stochastic pp-Laplace equation with nonlinear sources

(1.10) dXt=div(|∇Xt|p−2∇Xt)dt+λXt2dt+ℬ(t,Xt)dWt,dX_{t}=\text{div}(|\nabla X_{t}|^{p-2}\nabla X_{t})dt+\lambda X_{t}^{2}dt+\mathcal{B}(t,X_{t})dW_{t},

where λ=±1\lambda=\pm 1, Eq. (1.10) is degenerate if p>2p>2 or singular if 1<p<21<p<2. Nonlinear parabolic equation like (1.10) appears in various applications. For instance, in combustion theory, the function XtX_{t} represents the temperature, the term div(|∇Xt|p−2∇Xt)\text{div}(|\nabla X_{t}|^{p-2}\nabla X_{t}) represents the thermal diffusion, and the nonlinear source Xt2X_{t}^{2} is physically called the “hot source”, while the source −Xt2-X_{t}^{2} is known as the “cool source”. These different sources have completely different influences on the properties of solutions (cf. e.g. [14, 48, 64]). In the deterministic setting (i.e., ℬ⁡(t,u)≡0\mathcal{B}(t,u)\equiv 0) under the singular regime 1<p<21<p<2 and λ=1\lambda=1, solutions may blow up in finite time for some initial values, thereby there is no global-in-time solution (see e.g. [37, 48]). In this work, we demonstrate that the addition of suitable random noise can effectively prevent such blow-up.

More importantly, we discover a new phenomenon: for a deterministic model that exhibits blow-up, appropriate stochastic perturbations lead to the finite-time extinction of the stochastic counterpart. This result may shed new insight how noise affects the long-time behavior of stochastic systems.

1.3. Proof strategy

Now, we outline the main ideas of the proof. First, to construct a probabilistically weak solution to (1.2), we combine a stochastic compactness argument with techniques from the theory of pseudo-monotone operators. In contrast to existing works (cf. [40, 57]), under the generalized coercivity condition (1.5), we cannot guarantee that the Galerkin approximating solutions {X(n)}n∈ℕ\{X^{(n)}\}_{n\in\mathbb{N}} have finite second moments. Instead, we establish energy bounds of order 2−η02-\eta_{0} with η0∈(1,2)\eta_{0}\in(1,2) for {X(n)}n∈ℕ\{X^{(n)}\}_{n\in\mathbb{N}} by constructing a suitable Lyapunov function. Then, by employing a refined stopping time argument, we prove tightness in the space

𝒵T1:=C⁡([0,T],𝕍∗)∩Lα​([0,T],ℍ)∩Lwα​([0,T],𝕍),\mathcal{Z}^{1}_{T}:=C([0,T];\mathbb{V}^{*})\cap L^{\alpha}([0,T];\mathbb{H})\cap L^{\alpha}_{w}([0,T];\mathbb{V}),

where Lwα​([0,T],𝕍)L^{\alpha}_{w}([0,T];{\mathbb{V}}) denotes the space Lα​([0,T],𝕍)L^{\alpha}([0,T];{\mathbb{V}}) endowed with the weak topology.

Notably, the lack of finite second moments for {X(n)}n∈ℕ\{X^{(n)}\}_{n\in\mathbb{N}} introduces non-trivial technical difficulties in the proof. Specifically, we cannot follow the arguments in [40, 57] to obtain the weak convergence of the sequence {𝒜⁡(⋅,X⋅(n))}n∈ℕ\{\mathcal{A}(\cdot,X^{(n)}_{\cdot})\}_{n\in\mathbb{N}} or the convergence of the sequence {ℬ⁡(⋅,X⋅(n))}n∈ℕ\{\mathcal{B}(\cdot,X^{(n)}_{\cdot})\}_{n\in\mathbb{N}}. To address this, we establish the tightness of {𝒜⁡(⋅,X⋅(n))}n∈ℕ\{\mathcal{A}(\cdot,X^{(n)}_{\cdot})\}_{n\in\mathbb{N}} in the space

𝒵T2:=Lwαα−1​([0,T],𝕍∗).\mathcal{Z}^{2}_{T}:=L^{\frac{\alpha}{\alpha-1}}_{w}([0,T];\mathbb{V}^{*}).

Note that 𝒵T1\mathcal{Z}^{1}_{T} and 𝒵T2\mathcal{Z}^{2}_{T} are not Polish spaces. In this case, we apply the Jakubowski’s generalization of the Skorokhod representation theorem for nonmetric spaces, as presented by Brzeźniak and Ondreját [13]. This yields the almost sure convergence of both

{X(n)}n∈ℕ​and​{𝒜⁡(⋅,X⋅(n))}n∈ℕ\{X^{(n)}\}_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\penalty\ \text{and}\penalty\ \{\mathcal{A}(\cdot,X^{(n)}_{\cdot})\}_{n\in\mathbb{N}}

to limit elements X~\tilde{X} in 𝒵T1\mathcal{Z}^{1}_{T} and 𝒜~​(⋅)\tilde{\mathcal{A}}(\cdot) in 𝒵T2\mathcal{Z}^{2}_{T}, respectively, on a new probability space. To justify this step, it is crucial to prove that 𝒵T1\mathcal{Z}^{1}_{T} and 𝒵T2\mathcal{Z}^{2}_{T} are standard Borel spaces under an appropriate topology (cf. Remark 4.1 and Lemma 4.10 for details). Then, using a cut-off technique, we identify the limit and establish the strong convergence of ℬ⁡(⋅,X⋅(n))\mathcal{B}(\cdot,X^{(n)}_{\cdot}) to ℬ⁡(⋅,X~⋅)\mathcal{B}(\cdot,\tilde{X}_{\cdot}). Additionally, by exploiting the pseudo-monotonicity of 𝒜⁡(t,⋅)\mathcal{A}(t,\cdot), we establish the weak convergence of 𝒜⁡(⋅,X⋅(n))\mathcal{A}(\cdot,X^{(n)}_{\cdot}) to 𝒜⁡(⋅,X~⋅)\mathcal{A}(\cdot,\tilde{X}_{\cdot}).

However, it is noted that we only have estimates of order 2−η02-\eta_{0} for X~t\tilde{X}_{t}, the classical Itô’s formula (cf. Theorem 4.2.5 in [42]) within the variational framework cannot be directly applied. To overcome this difficulty, we utilize a refined stopping time technique combined with a localizaion procedure. Based on the Itô’s formula, we prove that X~∈C⁡([0,T],ℍ)\tilde{X}\in C([0,T];\mathbb{H}), which establishes that X~\tilde{X} is a probabilistically weak solution. Then, the existence of a unique probabilistically strong solution follows from pathwise uniqueness and the Yamada–Watanabe theorem.

1.4. Structure of the paper

The rest of paper is organized as follows. In Sect. 2, we introduce the main results about the existence, uniqueness, Feller property as well as finite-time extinction in Theorems 2.4-2.6, respectively. Then in Sec. 3, we apply our general framework to concrete examples to illustrate the wide applicability of the main results. In Sect. 4, we give the proofs of Theorems 2.4-2.6. We also recall some useful lemmas in the Appendix. Throughout this paper, CpC_{p} denotes some positive constant which may change from line to line, where the subscript pp is used to emphasize that the constant depends on certain parameter pp.

2. Main results

We recall some fundamental definitions and notations that are frequently used in the paper.

For any Banach space (𝔹,∥⋅∥𝔹)(\mathbb{B},\|\cdot\|_{\mathbb{B}}), we denote by ℂT​(𝔹):=C⁡([0,T],𝔹)\mathbb{C}_{T}(\mathbb{B}):=C([0,T];\mathbb{B}) the space of all continuous functions from [0,T][0,T] to 𝔹\mathbb{B}, which is a Banach space equipped with the uniform norm given by

‖u‖ℂT​(𝔹):=supt∈[0,T]‖ut‖𝔹,u∈ℂT​(𝔹).\|u\|_{\mathbb{C}_{T}(\mathbb{B})}:=\sup_{t\in[0,T]}\|u_{t}\|_{\mathbb{B}},\penalty\ u\in\mathbb{C}_{T}(\mathbb{B}).

Let ℬb​(𝔹)\mathscr{B}_{b}(\mathbb{B}) (resp. Cb​(𝔹)C_{b}(\mathbb{B})) be the space of all bounded and Borel measurable (resp. continuous) functions on 𝔹\mathbb{B}.

In this paper, we will employ the theory of pseudo-monotone operators. To this end, we first recall the definition of the pseudo-monotone operator. For abbreviation, we use the notation “⇀\rightharpoonup” for the weak convergence in a Banach space.

Definition 2.1.

An operator 𝒜\mathcal{A} from 𝕍\mathbb{V} to 𝕍∗\mathbb{V}^{*} is called to be a pseudo-monotone operator if un⇀uu_{n}\rightharpoonup u in 𝕍\mathbb{V} and

lim infn→∞⟨𝒜(un),un−u⟩𝕍𝕍∗≥0,\liminf_{n\to\infty}\,{}_{\mathbb{V}^{*}}\langle\mathcal{A}(u_{n}),u_{n}-u\rangle_{\mathbb{V}}\geq 0,

then for any v∈𝕍v\in\mathbb{V},

lim supn→∞⟨𝒜(un),un−v⟩𝕍𝕍∗≤𝕍∗⟨𝒜(u),u−v⟩𝕍.\limsup_{n\to\infty}\,{}_{\mathbb{V}^{*}}\langle\mathcal{A}(u_{n}),u_{n}-v\rangle_{\mathbb{V}}\leq\,_{\mathbb{V}^{*}}\langle\mathcal{A}(u),u-v\rangle_{\mathbb{V}}.
Remark 2.1.

Note that Browder [11] introduced a different definition of pseudo-monotone operator: An operator 𝒜\mathcal{A} from 𝕍\mathbb{V} to 𝕍∗\mathbb{V}^{*} is called pseudo-monotone if un⇀uu_{n}\rightharpoonup u in 𝕍\mathbb{V} and

lim infn→∞⟨𝒜(un),un−u⟩𝕍𝕍∗≥0\liminf_{n\to\infty}\,{}_{\mathbb{V}^{*}}\langle\mathcal{A}(u_{n}),u_{n}-u\rangle_{\mathbb{V}}\geq 0

implies 𝒜⁡(un)⇀𝒜⁡(u)\mathcal{A}(u_{n})\rightharpoonup\mathcal{A}(u) in 𝕍∗\mathbb{V}^{*} and

limn→∞⟨𝒜(un),un⟩𝕍𝕍∗=𝕍∗⟨𝒜(u),u⟩𝕍.\lim_{n\to\infty}\,{}_{\mathbb{V}^{*}}\langle\mathcal{A}(u_{n}),u_{n}\rangle_{\mathbb{V}}=\,_{\mathbb{V}^{*}}\langle\mathcal{A}(u),u\rangle_{\mathbb{V}}.

This definition turns out to be equivalent to Definition 2.3 (cf. [42, Remark 5.2.12]).

2.1. Well-posedness and Feller property

In this subsection, we consider the well-posedness and Feller property of SPDEs (1.2). To this end, we first recall the (probabilistically) weak and strong solutions to SPDEs (1.2) as follows.

Definition 2.2.

((Weak solution)) A pair (X,W)(X,W) is called a (probabilistically) weak solution to SPDE (1.2), if there exists (Ω,ℱ,{ℱt}t∈[0,T],ℙ)(\Omega,\mathscr{F},\{\mathscr{F}_{t}\}_{t\in[0,T]},\mathbb{P}) such that XX is an {ℱt}\{\mathscr{F}_{t}\}-adapted process and WW is an UU-valued cylindrical Wiener process on (Ω,ℱ,{ℱt}t∈[0,T],ℙ)(\Omega,\mathscr{F},\{\mathscr{F}_{t}\}_{t\in[0,T]},\mathbb{P}) and the following holds:

(i) X∈ℂT​(ℍ)X\in\mathbb{C}_{T}(\mathbb{H}), ℙ\mathbb{P}-a.s.;

(ii) ∫0T‖𝒜⁡(s,Xs)‖𝕍∗​𝑑s+∫0T‖ℬ⁡(s,Xs)‖L2​(U,ℍ)2​𝑑s<∞\int_{0}^{T}\|\mathcal{A}(s,X_{s})\|_{\mathbb{V}^{*}}ds+\int_{0}^{T}\|\mathcal{B}(s,X_{s})\|_{L_{2}(U;\mathbb{H})}^{2}ds<\infty, ℙ\mathbb{P}-a.s.;

(iii) Xt=X0+∫0t𝒜(s,Xs)ds+∫0tℬ(s,Xs)dWs,t∈[0,T],ℙ-a.s.X_{t}=X_{0}+\int_{0}^{t}\mathcal{A}(s,X_{s})ds+\int_{0}^{t}\mathcal{B}(s,X_{s})dW_{s},t\in[0,T],\mathbb{P}\text{-a.s.} holds in 𝕍∗{\mathbb{V}}^{*}.

Definition 2.3.

(Strong solution) We say that there exists a (probabilistically) strong solution to (1.2) if for every probability space (Ω,ℱ,{ℱt}t∈[0,T],ℙ)(\Omega,\mathscr{F},\{\mathscr{F}_{t}\}_{t\in[0,T]},\mathbb{P}) with an UU-valued cylindrical Wiener process WW, there exists an {ℱt}\{\mathscr{F}_{t}\}-adapted process XX such that properties (i)-(iii) in Definition 2.2 hold.

In this part, we suppose that there are some constants α>1\alpha>1, β≥2\beta\geq 2, and C,δ>0C,\delta>0 such that the following conditions hold for a.e. t∈[0,T]t\in[0,T].

  1. (𝐀𝟏)(\mathbf{A_{1}})

    ((Hemicontinuity)) For any u,v,w∈𝕍u,v,w\in{\mathbb{V}}, the map

    ℝ+∋λ↦𝕍∗⟨𝒜(t,u+λv),w⟩𝕍\mathbb{R}_{+}\ni\lambda\mapsto\penalty\ _{{\mathbb{V}}^{*}}\langle\mathcal{A}(t,u+\lambda v),w\rangle_{\mathbb{V}}

    is continuous.

    ((Local Monotonicity)) For any u,v∈𝕍u,v\in{\mathbb{V}},

    2𝕍∗​⟨𝒜⁡(t,u)−𝒜⁡(t,v),u−v⟩𝕍+‖ℬ⁡(t,u)−ℬ⁡(t,v)‖L2​(U,ℍ)2\displaystyle 2_{{\mathbb{V}}^{*}}\langle\mathcal{A}(t,u)-\mathcal{A}(t,v),u-v\rangle_{\mathbb{V}}+\|\mathcal{B}(t,u)-\mathcal{B}(t,v)\|_{L_{2}(U,{\mathbb{H}})}^{2}
    ≤(C+ρ⁡(u)+η⁡(v))​‖u−v‖ℍ2,\displaystyle\leq(C+\rho(u)+\eta(v))\|u-v\|_{\mathbb{H}}^{2},

We present the main result concerning the global existence, uniqueness, and Markov property of (probabilistically) strong solutions to SPDE (1.2).

Theorem 2.4.

Suppose that the embedding 𝕍⊂ℍ\mathbb{V}\subset\mathbb{H} is compact and that (𝐀𝟏)(\mathbf{A_{1}})-(𝐀𝟓)(\mathbf{A_{5}}) hold. For any initial data x∈ℍx\in\mathbb{H}, Eq. (1.2) has a unique strong solution in the sense of Definition 2.3. Moreover, we have the estimates

(2.6) supt∈[0,T]𝔼​‖Xt‖ℍ2−η0+𝔼​∫0T‖Xt‖𝕍α−η0​𝑑t<∞\sup_{t\in[0,T]}\mathbb{E}\|X_{t}\|_{\mathbb{H}}^{2-\eta_{0}}+\mathbb{E}\int_{0}^{T}\|X_{t}\|_{\mathbb{V}}^{\alpha-\eta_{0}}dt<\infty

and for any p≥2p\geq 2,

(2.7) ℙ⁡(supt∈[0,T]‖Xt‖ℍp+∫0T‖Xt‖𝕍α​𝑑t<∞)=1.\mathbb{P}\Bigg(\sup_{t\in[0,T]}\|X_{t}\|_{\mathbb{H}}^{p}+\int_{0}^{T}\|X_{t}\|_{\mathbb{V}}^{\alpha}dt<\infty\Bigg)=1.

Furthermore, if 𝒜⁡(t,⋅),ℬ⁡(t,⋅)\mathcal{A}(t,\cdot),\mathcal{B}(t,\cdot) are independent of t∈[0,T]t\in[0,T], then the solution (Xt)t∈[0,T](X_{t})_{t\in[0,T]} of Eq. (1.2) is a time-homogenous Markov process.

Remark 2.2.

The main results are applicable to various new stochastic models that cannot be treated by the classical variational framework established in [40, 46, 57, 66], such as stochastic 3D Navier-Stokes equations and stochastic surface growth models. Although these models fail to satisfy the classical coercivity condition (1.4), they do fit the generalized coercivity condition (𝐀𝟑)(\mathbf{A_{3}}) (see Section 3 for details).

Remark 2.3.

The generalized coercivity condition (𝐀𝟑)(\mathbf{A_{3}}) was first introduced by the last named author and Röckner in [41, 42], where they proved that Eq. (1.2) has a unique local solution under this condition in the case of additive noise (i.e. ℬ⁡(t,u)=ℬ⁡(t)\mathcal{B}(t,u)=\mathcal{B}(t)). Note that the main idea of the proof in [41, 42] is based on a shift transformation to reduce the SPDE (1.2) to a deterministic evolution equation with random coefficients. However, this strategy cannot handle the more general nonlinear multiplicative noise. More importantly, compared to [41, 42], we establish the global existence and uniqueness of solutions, rather than merely local ones.

Remark 2.4.

Condition (2.3) in (𝐀𝟓)(\mathbf{A_{5}}) plays an essential role in this work, as it balances the interplay between the effective component of the noise in the energy direction and the growth of nonlinear terms. This condition can be interpreted as follows:

  1. (i)

    When g⁡(x)=C0​xg(x)=C_{0}x, corresponding to the classical coercivity condition (1.4), the diffusion coefficient ℬ⁡(t,⋅)\mathcal{B}(t,\cdot) can exhibit both linear and superlinear growth.

  2. (ii)

    When g⁡(x)=C0​xpg(x)=C_{0}x^{p} with p>1p>1, the coefficient ℬ⁡(t,⋅)\mathcal{B}(t,\cdot) is required to exhibit superlinear growth.

This condition captures an anisotropic stabilizing mechanism: only the component of the noise acting in the energy direction contributes to the prevention of blow-up, see Remark 3.2 below for concrete applications in fluid mechanics.

Based on the existence and uniqueness of solutions to (1.2), we intend to investigate the continuous dependence on the initial data in probability (in other word, the well-posedness of Eq. (1.2)) and the Feller property of the associated transition semigroup.

where Xt​(x)X_{t}(x) is the solution to (1.2) with the initial data xx.

Based on Theorem 2.4, it is a direct consequence that (𝒯t)t≥0(\mathcal{T}_{t})_{t\geq 0} is a stochastically continuous Markov semigroup on ℬb​(ℍ)\mathscr{B}_{b}(\mathbb{H}).

Theorem 2.5.

Suppose that the embedding 𝕍⊂ℍ\mathbb{V}\subset\mathbb{H} is compact and that (𝐀𝟏)(\mathbf{A_{1}})-(𝐀𝟓)(\mathbf{A_{5}}) hold. In addition, suppose that for any u,v∈𝕍u,v\in\mathbb{V}, ℬ\mathcal{B} is locally Lipschitz in the sense that

Remark 2.6.

Since we have established the Feller property of the Markov semigroup (𝒯t)t≥0(\mathcal{T}_{t})_{t\geq 0} associated with (1.2), a natural and important question arises investigating the existence of an invariant measure. One commonly employed technique for establishing the existence of an invariant measure is the Krylov-Bogolyubov procedure. According to the criterion presented by Maslowski and Seidler [44], we need to prove the following estimate: for any ε>0\varepsilon>0 there exists R>0R>0 such that

(2.10) supT≥11T​∫0Tℙ⁡(‖Xt​(x)‖ℍ>R)​𝑑t<ε.\sup_{T\geq 1}\frac{1}{T}\int_{0}^{T}\mathbb{P}\big(\|X_{t}(x)\|_{\mathbb{H}}>R\big)dt<\varepsilon.

However, it is not sufficient to obtain (2.10) based on the estimate (4.9) below. This topic deserves further investigation in the future work.

2.2. Finite-time extinction

The phenomenon of finite-time extinction for stochastic fast diffusion equations (SFDEs) driven by linear multiplicative noise has been rigorously established in a series of pioneering works by Barbu, Da Prato, and Röckner [5, 6, 7, 8] and Gess [19]. This phenomenon is of profound physical and mathematical interest, as it provides a rigorous description of the relaxation dynamics characteristic of SOC.

Concerning finite-time extinction, the problem is generally divided into the following three cases:

  1. (i)

    Extinction with positive probability for small initial conditions;

  2. (ii)

    Extinction with positive probability for all initial values;

  3. (iii)

    Extinction with probability one for all initial values.

While Regimes (i) and (ii) present mathematically intriguing local or conditional behaviors, they do not fully capture the physical mechanism of SOC. In physical systems exhibiting SOC, relaxation to a stable state must be a deterministic event rather than a stochastic occurrence. Consequently, Regime (iii) aligns most closely with the physical paradigm of SOC, as it guarantees that the system always decays to zero in finite time almost surely.

The primary objective of this subsection is to establish a unified and general framework to investigate the almost sure finite-time extinction (i.e., Regime (iii)) of solutions to SPDEs (1.2) under the influence of potentially linear or nonlinear multiplicative noise. Specifically, one may anticipate that a structurally suitable noise will eventually dominate the underlying deterministic nonlinearities, thereby accelerating the decay of the system and driving it to extinction within a finite time horizon.

To explore this finite-time extinction, we suppose that there exist constants α∈(1,2)\alpha\in(1,2) and δ>0\delta>0 such that the following conditions hold for a.e. t∈[0,T]t\in[0,T].

  1. (𝐀𝟑∗)(\mathbf{A_{3}^{*}})

    ((Enhanced Coercivity)) For any u∈𝕍u\in\mathbb{V},

    2𝕍∗​⟨𝒜⁡(t,u),u⟩𝕍+δ​‖u‖𝕍α≤g⁡(‖u‖ℍ2),\displaystyle 2_{\mathbb{V}^{*}}\langle\mathcal{A}(t,u),u\rangle_{\mathbb{V}}+\delta\|u\|_{\mathbb{V}}^{\alpha}\leq g(\|u\|_{\mathbb{H}}^{2}),

    where the function gg is the same as in (𝐀𝟑)(\mathbf{A_{3}}) with g⁡(0)=0g(0)=0.

  2. (𝐀𝟓∗)(\mathbf{A_{5}^{*}})

    For any u∈𝕍u\in\mathbb{V},

    ‖ℬ⁡(t,u)‖L2​(U,ℍ)=0if‖u‖ℍ=0,\|\mathcal{B}(t,u)\|_{L_{2}(U,\mathbb{H})}=0\penalty\ \penalty\ \text{if}\penalty\ \penalty\ \|u\|_{\mathbb{H}}=0,

    and

    (2.11) (g⁡(‖u‖ℍ2)+‖ℬ⁡(t,u)‖L2​(U,ℍ)2)​‖u‖ℍ2≤α​‖ℬ​(t,u)∗​u‖U2.\big(g(\|u\|_{\mathbb{H}}^{2})+\|\mathcal{B}(t,u)\|_{L_{2}(U,\mathbb{H})}^{2}\big)\|u\|_{\mathbb{H}}^{2}\leq\alpha\|\mathcal{B}(t,u)^{*}u\|_{U}^{2}.
Remark 2.7.

Note that Assumption (2.11) is not comparable with Assumption (2.3). However, by choosing g⁡(x)=C0​xpg(x)=C_{0}x^{p}, it is easy to select a suitable diffusion coefficient satisfying both assumptions simultaneously, see Subsection 3.3 for details.

Let τe\tau_{e} be the following extinction time

τe:=inf{t≥0:‖Xt‖ℍ=0},\tau_{e}:=\inf\big\{t\geq 0:\|X_{t}\|_{\mathbb{H}}=0\big\},

where (Xt)t≥0(X_{t})_{t\geq 0} is the solution to (1.2) given by Theorem 2.4 with initial value x∈ℍx\in\mathbb{H}.

Theorem 2.6.

Suppose that the embedding 𝕍⊂ℍ\mathbb{V}\subset\mathbb{H} is compact and that (𝐀𝟏)(\mathbf{A_{1}}), (𝐀𝟐)(\mathbf{A_{2}}), (𝐀𝟑∗)(\mathbf{A_{3}^{*}}), (𝐀𝟒)(\mathbf{A_{4}}), (𝐀𝟓)(\mathbf{A_{5}}), and (𝐀𝟓∗)(\mathbf{A_{5}^{*}}) hold. Let the initial data x∈ℍx\in\mathbb{H}. Then for any t≥τet\geq\tau_{e},

(2.12) ‖Xt‖ℍ=0,ℙ​-a.s..\|X_{t}\|_{\mathbb{H}}=0,\penalty\ \mathbb{P}\text{-a.s.}.

Furthermore, there exists a constant c0>0c_{0}>0 such that for any T>0T>0,

(2.13) ℙ⁡(τe>T)≤c0​‖x‖ℍ2−αT.\mathbb{P}(\tau_{e}>T)\leq\frac{c_{0}\|x\|_{\mathbb{H}}^{2-\alpha}}{T}.

Moreover, we also have the moment estimate of the extinction time

(2.14) 𝔼​τe≤c0​‖x‖ℍ2−α.\mathbb{E}\tau_{e}\leq c_{0}\|x\|_{\mathbb{H}}^{2-\alpha}.
Remark 2.8.

(i) Compared with the existing works [5, 6, 7, 8], the above theorem provides quantitative estimates for the extinction time, which derive the almost sure finite-time extinction (i.e., Regime (iii)) of solutions to SPDEs (1.2). Furthermore, the constant c0c_{0} has an explicit representation depending on the embedding constant of 𝕍⊂ℍ\mathbb{V}\subset\mathbb{H} (see Subsection 4.6 for details).

As a result, while previous studies (e.g. [5, 6, 7, 8, 19]) were limited to linear multiplicative noise, we establish, for the first time, finite-time extinction for a class of quasilinear SPDEs driven by nonlinear multiplicative noise, encompassing stochastic fast diffusion equations and stochastic singular pp-Laplace equations (with source terms).

(ii) In a forthcoming work, we aim to investigate finite-time extinction for SOC models (e.g., the BTW model and the Zhang model) perturbed by nonlinear multiplicative noise, which describe dynamical systems possessing a critical point as an attractor.

    ‖ℬ⁡(t,u)‖L2​(U,ℍ)=0if‖u‖ℍ=0,\|\mathcal{B}(t,u)\|_{L_{2}(U,\mathbb{H})}=0\penalty\ \penalty\ \text{if}\penalty\ \penalty\ \|u\|_{\mathbb{H}}=0,

As discussed in Remark 2.2, a typical choice of function gg in infinite-dimensional applications is

g⁡(x)=C0​xpwithp>1,C0>0.g(x)=C_{0}x^{p}\penalty\ \penalty\ \text{with}\penalty\ \penalty\ p>1,C_{0}>0.

Example. The diffusion coefficient can be constructed as follows:

(i) For y∈Uy\in U, we define

(3.2) ℬ⁡(t,u)​y:=∑k=1∞bk​‖u‖ℍm​u​⟨y,gk⟩U,\mathcal{B}(t,u)y:=\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}b_{k}\|u\|_{\mathbb{H}}^{m}u\langle y,g_{k}\rangle_{U},

γ:=∑k=1∞bk2<∞.\gamma:=\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}b_{k}^{2}<\infty.

For the reader’s convenience, we provide a detailed proof showing that Example 3.2 satisfies condition (𝐀ℬ2)(\mathbf{A}^{2}_{\mathcal{B}}) when m=p−1m=p-1.

By the definition of the adjoint operator ℬ​(t,u)∗\mathcal{B}(t,u)^{*}, we have

=\displaystyle=\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\! ⟨u,ℬ⁡(t,u)​ℬ​(t,u)∗​u⟩ℍ\displaystyle\langle u,\mathcal{B}(t,u)\mathcal{B}(t,u)^{*}u\rangle_{\mathbb{H}}
=\displaystyle=\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\! ∑k=1∞bk​‖u‖ℍp−1​⟨u,u⟩ℍ​⟨ℬ​(t,u)∗​u,gk⟩U\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}b_{k}\|u\|_{\mathbb{H}}^{p-1}\langle u,u\rangle_{\mathbb{H}}\langle\mathcal{B}(t,u)^{*}u,g_{k}\rangle_{U}

=\displaystyle=\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\! γ​‖u‖ℍ2​p+2.\displaystyle\gamma\|u\|_{\mathbb{H}}^{2p+2}.

For a large constant γ\gamma, we can obtain that there exists η0∈(1,2)\eta_{0}\in(1,2),

(g⁡(‖u‖ℍ2)+‖ℬ⁡(t,u)‖L2​(U,ℍ)2)​(1+‖u‖ℍ2)≤\displaystyle\big(g(\|u\|_{\mathbb{H}}^{2})+\|\mathcal{B}(t,u)\|_{L_{2}({U},{\mathbb{H}})}^{2}\big)(1+\|u\|_{\mathbb{H}}^{2})\leq\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\! (C0​‖u‖ℍ2​p+γ​‖u‖ℍ2​p)​(1+‖u‖ℍ2)\displaystyle(C_{0}\|u\|_{\mathbb{H}}^{2p}+\gamma\|u\|_{\mathbb{H}}^{2p})(1+\|u\|_{\mathbb{H}}^{2})

(ii) In particular, this setup applies to the case of a one-dimensional Wiener process. For u∈ℍu\in\mathbb{H} and y∈Uy\in U, choosing bk=c​δ1,kb_{k}=c\delta_{1,k} with a constant c≠0c\neq 0 yields

(3.3) ℬ⁡(t,u)​y:=c​‖u‖ℍm​u​⟨y,g1⟩U.\mathcal{B}(t,u)y:=c\|u\|_{\mathbb{H}}^{m}u\langle y,g_{1}\rangle_{U}.

Remark 3.1.

The above example represents a class of nonlocal forcing terms that characterize the spatial dependence of systems arising in engineering, biology, and fluid mechanics. Such nonlocal mechanisms have been widely investigated in the study of deterministic PDEs, including non-degenerate Kirchhoff-type forcing in wave equations (cf. [32]) and Woinowsky-Krieger nonlocal forcing for extensible beams (cf. [70] or [31, Section 6]). We refer the reader to Remark 3.2 for a more detailed discussion within mathematical fluid mechanics.

3.1. Stochastic 3D Navier-Stokes equations

3D Navier-Stokes system is a classical model to describe the time evolution of an incompressible fluid (cf. [35, 63, 72]), which is given as follows

(3.4) {∂tu=νΔu−(u⋅∇)u−∇p+f,div(u)=0,u|∂Λ=0,u(0)=u0,\displaystyle\left\{\begin{aligned} &\partial_{t}{u}=\nu\Delta{u}-(u\cdot{\nabla})u-\nabla{p}+f,\\ &\text{div}(u)=0,u|_{\partial\Lambda}=0,u(0)=u_{0},\end{aligned}\right.

where uu represents the velocity field of the fluid, ν>0\nu>0 is the viscosity constant, pp denotes the pressure, and ff is an external force field acting on the fluid.

Define

Hm:={v∈W0m,2​(Λ,ℝ3):div​(v)=0}.H^{m}:=\Big\{v\in W_{0}^{m,2}(\Lambda;\mathbb{R}^{3}):\text{div}(v)=0\Big\}.

Identifying H1H^{1} with its dual space by the Riesz isomorphism, then we will use the following Gelfand triple

(3.5) 𝕍:=H2⊂ℍ:=H1⊂𝕍∗.\mathbb{V}:=H^{2}\subset\mathbb{H}:=H^{1}\subset{\mathbb{V}}^{*}.

Let 𝒫ℍ\mathcal{P}_{\mathbb{H}} be the orthogonal projection operator on L2​(Λ,ℝ3)L^{2}(\Lambda;\mathbb{R}^{3}) onto H0H^{0}, which is called the Leray-Helmholtz projection. Then, the classical 3D Navier-Stokes system (3.4) can be reformulated in the following abstract form

(3.6) ∂tu=A​u+B⁡(u)+F,u⁡(0)=u0,\partial_{t}u=Au+B(u)+F,\penalty\ \penalty\ \penalty\ u(0)=u_{0},

where operators

A:𝕍→𝕍∗,A​u:=ν​Pℍ​Δ​u,A:\mathbb{V}\rightarrow{\mathbb{V}}^{*},\penalty\ \penalty\ \penalty\ Au:=\nu P_{\mathbb{H}}\Delta{u},
B:𝕍×𝕍→𝕍∗,B(u,v):=Pℍ[(u⋅∇)v],B(u):=B(u,u)B:\mathbb{V}\times\mathbb{V}\rightarrow{\mathbb{V}}^{*},\penalty\ \penalty\ \penalty\ B(u,v):=P_{\mathbb{H}}[(u\cdot{\nabla})v],\penalty\ \penalty\ B(u):=B(u,u)
F:[0,T]→H0,Ft=𝒫ℍ​ftF:[0,T]\rightarrow H^{0},\penalty\ \penalty\ \penalty\ F_{t}=\mathcal{P}_{\mathbb{H}}f_{t}

are well-defined.

Over the past few decades, the 3D Navier-Stokes equations have been intensively studied in the literature. However, their global well-posedness remains a challenging open problem. Motivated by this, we are interested in the following stochastic 3D Navier-Stokes equations:

(3.7) d​Xt=[A​Xt+B⁡(Xt)]​d​t+ℬ⁡(t,Xt)​d​Wt,X0=x,\displaystyle d{X_{t}}=\big[AX_{t}+B(X_{t})\big]dt+\mathcal{B}(t,X_{t})dW_{t},\penalty\ X_{0}=x,

where {Wt}t∈[0,T]\{W_{t}\}_{t\in[0,T]} is an UU-valued cylindrical Wiener process with UU being a separable Hilbert space, and the diffusion coefficient ℬ\mathcal{B} satisfies (𝐀ℬ1)(\mathbf{A}^{1}_{\mathcal{B}}) and (𝐀ℬ2)(\mathbf{A}^{2}_{\mathcal{B}}) with g⁡(x)=C​x3g(x)=Cx^{3} for a large constant CC.

Theorem 3.1.

For any initial data x∈H1x\in H^{1}, Eq. (3.7) has a unique strong solution. Moreover, we have the estimate

supt∈[0,T]𝔼​‖Xt‖12−η0+𝔼​∫0T‖Xt‖22−η0​𝑑t<∞.\sup_{t\in[0,T]}\mathbb{E}\|X_{t}\|_{1}^{2-\eta_{0}}+\mathbb{E}\int_{0}^{T}\|X_{t}\|_{2}^{2-\eta_{0}}dt<\infty.

Furthermore, let Xt​(x)X_{t}(x) be the unique solution to Eq. (3.7) with the initial data xx, {xn}n∈ℕ\{x_{n}\}_{n\in\mathbb{N}} and xx be a sequence with ‖xn−x‖1→0\|x_{n}-x\|_{1}\to 0, then

‖X⁡(xn)−X⁡(x)‖ℂT​(H1)→0in probability asn→∞.\|X(x_{n})-X(x)\|_{\mathbb{C}_{T}(H^{1})}\to 0\penalty\ \penalty\ \text{in probability as}\penalty\ \penalty\ n\to\infty.

In particular, the corresponding Markov semigroup (𝒯t)t≥0(\mathcal{T}_{t})_{t\geq 0} is a Feller semigroup in Cb​(H1)C_{b}(H^{1}).

Proof.

By Theorems 2.4 and 2.5, we only need to verify that the conditions (𝐀𝟏)(\mathbf{A_{1}})-(𝐀𝟒)(\mathbf{A_{4}}) hold for Eq. (3.7).

Let

𝒜⁡(t,u):=A​u+B⁡(u).\mathcal{A}(t,u):=Au+B(u).

The proof of the conditions (𝐀𝟏)(\mathbf{A_{1}})-(𝐀𝟒)(\mathbf{A_{4}}) for 𝒜\mathcal{A} is similar to that of Example 5.2.23 in [42], we include it here for completeness.

The hemicontinuity (𝐀𝟏)(\mathbf{A_{1}}) is obvious since BB is a bilinear map.

By the Agmon inequality (see e.g. (A.29) in [18]),

(3.8) ‖u‖L∞≤C​‖u‖112​‖u‖212,u∈H2,\displaystyle\|u\|_{L^{\infty}}\leq C\|u\|_{1}^{\frac{1}{2}}\|u\|_{2}^{\frac{1}{2}},\penalty\ u\in H^{2},

we have

⟨B(u)−B(v),u−v⟩𝕍𝕍∗\displaystyle{}_{\mathbb{V}^{*}}{\langle}B(u)-B(v),u-v{\rangle}_{\mathbb{V}}
=\displaystyle=\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\! ⟨B⁡(u)−B⁡(v),(−Δ)​(u−v)⟩L2\displaystyle{\langle}B(u)-B(v),(-\Delta)(u-v){\rangle}_{L^{2}}
≤\displaystyle\leq\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\! ∥u−v∥2∥(u⋅∇)u−(v⋅∇)v∥L2\displaystyle\|u-v\|_{2}\|(u\cdot\nabla)u-(v\cdot\nabla)v\|_{L^{2}}
≤\displaystyle\leq\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\! ‖u−v‖2​(‖u‖L∞​‖∇u−∇v‖L2+‖u−v‖L∞​‖∇v‖L2)\displaystyle\|u-v\|_{2}\left(\|u\|_{L^{\infty}}\|\nabla u-\nabla v\|_{L^{2}}+\|u-v\|_{L^{\infty}}\|\nabla v\|_{L^{2}}\right)
≤\displaystyle\leq\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\! ‖u−v‖2​(‖u‖L∞​‖u−v‖1+C​‖u−v‖21/2​‖u−v‖11/2​‖v‖1)\displaystyle\|u-v\|_{2}\left(\|u\|_{L^{\infty}}\|u-v\|_{1}+C\|u-v\|_{2}^{1/2}\|u-v\|_{1}^{1/2}\|v\|_{1}\right)
≤\displaystyle\leq\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\! ν2​‖u−v‖22+C⁡(‖u‖2​‖u‖1+‖v‖14)​‖u−v‖12,u,v∈𝕍,\displaystyle\frac{\nu}{2}\|u-v\|_{2}^{2}+C\left(\|u\|_{2}\|u\|_{1}+\|v\|_{1}^{4}\right)\|u-v\|_{1}^{2},\ u,v\in{\mathbb{V}},

then

𝕍∗⟨Au+B(u)−Av−B(v),u−v⟩𝕍≤−ν2​‖u−v‖22+C⁡(‖u‖2​‖u‖1+‖v‖14)​‖u−v‖12,u,v∈𝕍,\begin{split}&{}_{\mathbb{V}^{*}}{\langle}Au+B(u)-Av-B(v),u-v{\rangle}_{\mathbb{V}}\\ \leq&-\frac{\nu}{2}\|u-v\|_{2}^{2}+C\left(\|u\|_{2}\|u\|_{1}+\|v\|_{1}^{4}\right)\|u-v\|_{1}^{2},\ u,v\in{\mathbb{V}},\end{split}

which implies the local monotonicity (𝐀𝟐)(\mathbf{A_{2}}) holds with α=2,β=m\alpha=2,\beta=m and

ρ⁡(u):=C​‖u‖2​‖u‖1,η⁡(v)=C​‖v‖14.\rho(u):=C\|u\|_{2}\|u\|_{1},\penalty\ \penalty\ \eta(v)=C\|v\|_{1}^{4}.

In particular, there exists a constant C>0C>0 such that

⟨Au+B(u),u⟩𝕍𝕍∗≤−ν2∥u∥22+C(1+∥u∥16),u∈𝕍.{}_{\mathbb{V}^{*}}{\langle}Au+B(u),u{\rangle}_{\mathbb{V}}\leq-\frac{\nu}{2}\|u\|_{2}^{2}+C(1+\|u\|_{1}^{6}),\ u\in{\mathbb{V}}.

Then, (𝐀𝟑)(\mathbf{A_{3}}) holds with g⁡(x)=C​x3g(x)=Cx^{3}, i.e.,

⟨𝒜(t,u),v⟩𝕍𝕍∗≤−ν2∥u∥22+g(∥u∥12)+C,u∈𝕍.{}_{\mathbb{V}^{*}}{\langle}\mathcal{A}(t,u),v{\rangle}_{\mathbb{V}}\leq-\frac{\nu}{2}\|u\|_{2}^{2}+g(\|u\|_{1}^{2})+C,\ u\in{\mathbb{V}}.

Concerning the growth condition, by (3.8) we have

∥B(u)∥𝕍∗2≤∥(u⋅∇)u∥L22≤∥u∥L∞2∥∇u∥L22≤C∥u∥2∥u∥13≤C∥u∥22∥u∥12,u∈𝕍.\|B(u)\|_{\mathbb{V}^{*}}^{2}\leq\|(u\cdot\nabla)u\|_{L^{2}}^{2}\leq\|u\|_{L^{\infty}}^{2}\|\nabla u\|_{L^{2}}^{2}\leq C\|u\|_{2}\|u\|_{1}^{3}\leq C\|u\|_{2}^{2}\|u\|_{1}^{2},\ u\in{\mathbb{V}}.

Hence, (𝐀𝟒)(\mathbf{A_{4}}) holds. The proof is completed. ∎

Remark 3.2.

As discussed in Remark 3.1, the main results established in Theorem 3.1 are applicable to the following class of nonlocal stochastic perturbations

(3.9) ∫0tℬ⁡(s,us)​d​Ws:=∑k=1∞∫0tbk​us​∫Λ|∇us​(ξ)|2​𝑑ξ​d​βk​(s),\int_{0}^{t}\mathcal{B}(s,u_{s})dW_{s}:=\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\int_{0}^{t}b_{k}u_{s}\int_{\Lambda}|\nabla u_{s}(\xi)|^{2}d\xi d\beta_{k}(s),

where γ:=∑k=1∞bk2\gamma:=\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}b_{k}^{2} is a large constant, {βk​(t)}k∈ℕ\{\beta_{k}(t)\}_{k\in\mathbb{N}} is a sequence of independent one-dimensional standard Wiener processes. Physically, the nonlocal stochastic forcing (3.9)(\ref{exaB1}) characterizes spatially dependent random perturbations whose intensity is modulated by the total energy dissipation of the system.

Such integral-type nonlocal operators plays an important role in mathematical fluid mechanics. In the celebrated paper [34], Ladyzenskaja introduced Navier-Stokes equations with this class of deterministic nonlocal viscosity forces, which is related to the total dissipation energy of Newtonian fluid. Moreover, as noted in [15], this type of nonlocal viscosity allows one to interpret the system as the asymptotic limit of certain nonisothermal flows characterized by high thermal conductivity.

Remark 3.3.

(i) Although stochastic Navier-Stokes equations have been intensively studied over the past few decades (cf. e.g. [17, 49, 59]), the global well-posedness of the stochastic 3D Navier-Stokes equations has not yet been fully resolved. Applying our general framework, we establish that the stochastic 3D Navier-Stokes system (3.7) driven by a class of nonlinear multiplicative noises is globally well-posed for general H1H^{1} initial data.

(ii) It is well established that the 2D Navier-Stokes equations fit the classical local monotonicity framework (cf. [40]) based on the Gelfand triple

𝕍:=H1⊂ℍ:=H0⊂𝕍∗.\mathbb{V}:=H^{1}\subset\mathbb{H}:=H^{0}\subset\mathbb{V}^{*}.

However, this Gelfand triple does not apply to the 3D setting. To address this issue, we introduce an alternative Gelfand triple (3.5) in Theorem 3.1, which serves as the appropriate framework.

3.2. Stochastic surface growth models

In this subsection, we apply our general framework to study the following 1D surface growth model

(3.10) {∂tu=−∂x4u−∂x2u+∂x2(∂xu)2,u|∂Λ=0,u(0)=u0,\displaystyle\left\{\begin{aligned} &\partial_{t}{u}=-\partial_{x}^{4}u-\partial_{x}^{2}u+\partial_{x}^{2}(\partial_{x}u)^{2},\\ &u|_{\partial\Lambda}=0,u(0)=u_{0},\end{aligned}\right.

where ∂x,∂x2,∂x4\partial_{x},\partial_{x}^{2},\partial_{x}^{4} denote the first, second and fourth spatial derivatives, respectively. This model appears in the theory of growth of surfaces, which describes an amorphous material deposited on an initially flat surface in high vacuum (cf. [53]).

Owing to the highly nonlinear nature of model (3.10), global well-posedness for the 1D surface growth model has not yet been resolved in either the deterministic or stochastic settings. In particular, this model is known to share comparable difficulties with the 3D Navier–Stokes equations.

Taking random noise into account, the equation is formulated as follows

(3.11) {dXt=[−∂x4Xt−∂x2Xt+∂x2(∂xXt)2]dt+ℬ(t,Xt)dWt,Xt|∂Λ=0,\displaystyle\left\{\begin{aligned} &dX_{t}=\left[-\partial_{x}^{4}X_{t}-\partial_{x}^{2}X_{t}+\partial_{x}^{2}(\partial_{x}X_{t})^{2}\right]dt+\mathcal{B}(t,X_{t})dW_{t},\\ &X_{t}|_{\partial\Lambda}=0,\end{aligned}\right.

where the diffusion coefficient ℬ\mathcal{B} satisfies (𝐀ℬ1)(\mathbf{A}^{1}_{\mathcal{B}}) and (𝐀ℬ2)(\mathbf{A}^{2}_{\mathcal{B}}) with g⁡(x)=C​x3g(x)=Cx^{3} for a large constant CC.

We take the following Gelfand triple to obtain the global well-posedness of Eq. (3.11), i.e.,

𝕍:=W04,2​(Λ,ℝ)⊂ℍ:=W02,2​(Λ,ℝ)⊂𝕍∗.\mathbb{V}:=W_{0}^{4,2}(\Lambda;\mathbb{R})\subset\mathbb{H}:=W_{0}^{2,2}(\Lambda;\mathbb{R})\subset{\mathbb{V}}^{*}.
Theorem 3.2.

For any initial data x∈W02,2x\in W_{0}^{2,2}, Eq. (3.11) has a unique strong solution. Moreover, we have the estimate

supt∈[0,T]𝔼​‖Xt‖22−η0+𝔼​∫0T‖Xt‖42−η0​𝑑t<∞.\sup_{t\in[0,T]}\mathbb{E}\|X_{t}\|_{2}^{2-\eta_{0}}+\mathbb{E}\int_{0}^{T}\|X_{t}\|_{4}^{2-\eta_{0}}dt<\infty.

Furthermore, let Xt​(x)X_{t}(x) be the unique solution to Eq. (3.11) with the initial data xx, {xn}n∈ℕ\{x_{n}\}_{n\in\mathbb{N}} and xx be a sequence with ‖xn−x‖2→0\|x_{n}-x\|_{2}\to 0, then

‖X⁡(xn)−X⁡(x)‖ℂT​(W02,2)→0in probability asn→∞.\|X(x_{n})-X(x)\|_{\mathbb{C}_{T}(W_{0}^{2,2})}\to 0\penalty\ \penalty\ \text{in probability as}\penalty\ \penalty\ n\to\infty.

In particular, the corresponding Markov semigroup (𝒯t)t≥0(\mathcal{T}_{t})_{t\geq 0} is a Feller semigroup in Cb​(W02,2)C_{b}(W_{0}^{2,2}).

Proof.

The conditions (𝐀𝟏)(\mathbf{A_{1}})-(𝐀𝟓)(\mathbf{A_{5}}) hold for Eq. (3.11) with g⁡(x)=C​x3g(x)=Cx^{3}, whose proof follows from Section 3.4 in [41], we omit the details. ∎

Remark 3.4.

The solution obtained here for the stochastic surface growth model is a global strong solution in both the PDE and probability senses. We note that the local existence of solutions for this model has been established in [41, 60]. To the best of our knowledge, Theorem 3.2 provides the first global well-posedness result for the stochastic surface growth model.

Our general framework is not restricted to the aforementioned semi-linear SPDEs; it also encompasses a wide class of quasi-linear stochastic dynamics, including stochastic pp-Laplace equations (with heat sources) and stochastic fast-diffusion equations.

3.3. Stochastic singular pp-Laplace equations with heat sources

In this subsection, we investigate the finite-time extinction of solutions to stochastic 1D singular pp-Laplace equations with nonlinear sources. Specifically, we consider the following deterministic equation

(3.12) {∂tu=div(|∇u|p−2∇u)+u2,u|∂Λ=0,u(0)=u0,\displaystyle\left\{\begin{aligned} &\partial_{t}{u}=\text{div}(|\nabla u|^{p-2}\nabla u)+u^{2},\\ &u|_{\partial\Lambda}=0,u(0)=u_{0},\end{aligned}\right.

where 1<p<21<p<2. This model arises in combustion theory, where uu represents the temperature, the term div(|∇u|p−2∇u)\operatorname{div}(|\nabla u|^{p-2}\nabla u) denotes thermal diffusion, and the nonlinear source u2u^{2} is physically referred to as a “hot source” (cf. e.g. [14, 48, 64]).

It is well known that solutions to (3.12) may blow up in finite time under certain initial conditions. Thus, global solutions do not exist in general (see, e.g., [37, 48]). Taking random noise into account, we study the following stochastic singular pp-Laplace equation

(3.13) {dXt=[div(|∇Xt|p−2∇Xt)+Xt2]dt+ℬ(t,Xt)dWt,Xt|∂Λ=0,\displaystyle\left\{\begin{aligned} &dX_{t}=[\text{div}(|\nabla X_{t}|^{p-2}\nabla X_{t})+X_{t}^{2}]dt+\mathcal{B}(t,X_{t})dW_{t},\\ &X_{t}|_{\partial\Lambda}=0,\end{aligned}\right.

where the diffusion coefficient ℬ\mathcal{B} satisfies (𝐀ℬ1)(\mathbf{A}^{1}_{\mathcal{B}}), (𝐀ℬ2)(\mathbf{A}^{2}_{\mathcal{B}}), and (𝐀ℬ2∗)(\mathbf{A}^{2*}_{\mathcal{B}}) with g⁡(x)=C​x4​p−33​p−3g(x)=Cx^{\frac{4p-3}{3p-3}} for a large constant CC.

To analyze (3.13), we employ the Gelfand triple

𝕍:=W01,p​(Λ,ℝ)⊂ℍ:=L2​(Λ,ℝ)⊂𝕍∗.\mathbb{V}:=W_{0}^{1,p}(\Lambda;\mathbb{R})\subset\mathbb{H}:=L^{2}(\Lambda;\mathbb{R})\subset\mathbb{V}^{*}.
Theorem 3.3.

For any initial data x∈L2x\in L^{2}, Eq. (3.13) has a unique strong solution. Moreover, we have the estimate

supt∈[0,T]𝔼​‖Xt‖L22−η0+𝔼​∫0T‖Xt‖W1,p2−η0​𝑑t<∞.\sup_{t\in[0,T]}\mathbb{E}\|X_{t}\|_{L^{2}}^{2-\eta_{0}}+\mathbb{E}\int_{0}^{T}\|X_{t}\|_{W^{1,p}}^{2-\eta_{0}}dt<\infty.

Furthermore, let {xn}n∈ℕ\{x_{n}\}_{n\in\mathbb{N}} and xx be a sequence with ‖xn−x‖L2→0\|x_{n}-x\|_{L^{2}}\to 0. Let Xt​(x)X_{t}(x) be the unique solution to Eq. (3.13) with the initial data xx. Then

‖X⁡(xn)−X⁡(x)‖ℂT​(L2)→0in probability asn→∞.\|X(x_{n})-X(x)\|_{\mathbb{C}_{T}(L^{2})}\to 0\penalty\ \penalty\ \text{in probability as}\penalty\ \penalty\ n\to\infty.

In particular, the corresponding Markov semigroup (𝒯t)t≥0(\mathcal{T}_{t})_{t\geq 0} is a Feller semigroup in Cb​(L2)C_{b}(L^{2}).

Proof.

Let

𝒜(t,u):=div(|∇u|p−2∇u)+u2.\mathcal{A}(t,u):=\text{div}(|\nabla u|^{p-2}\nabla u)+u^{2}.

For any u,v∈𝕍u,v\in{\mathbb{V}}, by Young’s inequality we have

Let τe\tau_{e} be the extinction time defined by

(3.15) τe:=inf{t≥0:‖Xt‖L2=0},\tau_{e}:=\inf\big\{t\geq 0:\|X_{t}\|_{L^{2}}=0\big\},

where (Xt)t≥0(X_{t})_{t\geq 0} is the solution to (3.13) with initial value X0=x∈L2X_{0}=x\in L^{2}. We establish the following finite-time extinction result for (3.13).

Theorem 3.4.

For any initial data x∈L2x\in L^{2}, we have

‖Xt‖L2=0for all ​t≥τe,ℙ​-a.s.\|X_{t}\|_{L^{2}}=0\quad\text{for all }t\geq\tau_{e},\ \mathbb{P}\text{-a.s.}

Furthermore, there exists a constant c0>0c_{0}>0 such that for any T>0T>0,

ℙ⁡(τe>T)≤c0​‖x‖L22−pT.\mathbb{P}(\tau_{e}>T)\leq\frac{c_{0}\|x\|_{L^{2}}^{2-p}}{T}.

Moreover, we also have the moment estimate of the extinction time

𝔼​τe≤c0​‖x‖L22−p.\mathbb{E}\tau_{e}\leq c_{0}\|x\|_{L^{2}}^{2-p}.
Proof.

It suffices to verify condition (𝐀𝟑∗)(\mathbf{A_{3}^{*}}), which follows directly from (3.14). ∎

Remark 3.5.

Note that solutions of the deterministic singular pp-Laplace equation (3.12) may blow up in finite time. We show that the introduction of appropriate random noise can induce almost sure finite-time extinction for the stochastic dynamics. This is a novel phenomenon that illustrates the effect of random noise on the long-time behavior of singular pp-Laplace equations.

3.4. Stochastic fast diffusion equations

The fast diffusion equation arises in the description of a wide variety of physical phenomena and processes, including fluid flows in porous media, diffusion processes in kinetic gas theory, heat transfer in plasmas, and population dynamics (cf. [7, 19]).

In this subsection, we study SFDEs. We assume either d∈{1,2}d\in\{1,2\} with r∈(0,1)r\in(0,1), or d≥3d\geq 3 with r∈[d−2d+2,1)r\in\left[\frac{d-2}{d+2},1\right). Specifically, we consider

(3.16) {d​Xt=Δ⁡(|Xt|r−1​Xt)​d​t+ℬ⁡(t,Xt)​d​Wt,Xt|∂Λ=0,\displaystyle\left\{\begin{aligned} &dX_{t}=\Delta(|X_{t}|^{r-1}X_{t})dt+\mathcal{B}(t,X_{t})dW_{t},\\ &X_{t}|_{\partial\Lambda}=0,\end{aligned}\right.

where the diffusion coefficient ℬ\mathcal{B} satisfies (𝐀ℬ1)(\mathbf{A}^{1}_{\mathcal{B}}) and (𝐀ℬ2)(\mathbf{A}^{2}_{\mathcal{B}}) with g⁡(x)=0g(x)=0.

We employ the Gelfand triple

𝕍:=Lr+1​(Λ,ℝ)⊂ℍ:=H−1​(Λ,ℝ)⊂𝕍∗,\mathbb{V}:=L^{r+1}(\Lambda;\mathbb{R})\subset\mathbb{H}:=H^{-1}(\Lambda;\mathbb{R})\subset\mathbb{V}^{*},

where H−1​(Λ,ℝ)H^{-1}(\Lambda;\mathbb{R}) denotes the dual space of W01,2​(Λ,ℝ)W_{0}^{1,2}(\Lambda;\mathbb{R}), associated with the norm ∥⋅∥−1\|\cdot\|_{-1}.

Next, we establish the finite-time extinction of solutions to stochastic fast diffusion equations. Let τe\tau_{e} be the extinction time defined by

τe:=inf{t≥0:‖Xt‖−1=0},\tau_{e}:=\inf\big\{t\geq 0:\|X_{t}\|_{-1}=0\big\},

where (Xt)t≥0(X_{t})_{t\geq 0} is the solution to (3.16) with initial value X0=x∈H−1X_{0}=x\in H^{-1}. We present the following result.

Theorem 3.5.

For any initial data x∈H−1x\in H^{-1}, we have

‖Xt‖−1=0for all ​t≥τe,ℙ​-a.s.\|X_{t}\|_{-1}=0\quad\text{for all }t\geq\tau_{e},\ \mathbb{P}\text{-a.s.}

Furthermore, there exists a constant c0>0c_{0}>0 such that for any T>0T>0,

ℙ⁡(τe>T)≤c0​‖x‖−12−pT.\mathbb{P}(\tau_{e}>T)\leq\frac{c_{0}\|x\|_{-1}^{2-p}}{T}.

Moreover, we also have the moment estimate of the extinction time

𝔼​τe≤c0​‖x‖−12−p.\mathbb{E}\tau_{e}\leq c_{0}\|x\|_{-1}^{2-p}.
Proof.

It is well known that the operator 𝒜⁡(t,u):=Δ⁡(|u|r−1​u)\mathcal{A}(t,u):=\Delta(|u|^{r-1}u) satisfies conditions (𝐀1)(\mathbf{A}_{1})–(𝐀5)(\mathbf{A}_{5}) with g≡0g\equiv 0; we refer to [42, Example 4.1.11] for details. By applying Theorem 2.6, the assertion follows. ∎

Remark 3.6.

We note that Theorem 3.5 applies to the finite-time extinction of SFDEs driven by linear multiplicative noise, a setting commonly considered in the existing literature (cf. [5, 6, 7, 8, 19]), i.e.,

Xt=x+∫0tΔ⁡(|Xs|r−1​Xs)​𝑑s+∑k=1∞∫0tbk​Xs​d​βk​(s),X_{t}=x+\int_{0}^{t}\Delta(|X_{s}|^{r-1}X_{s})ds+\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\int_{0}^{t}b_{k}X_{s}d\beta_{k}(s),

where ∑k=1∞bk2<∞\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}b_{k}^{2}<\infty and {βk​(t)}k∈ℕ\{\beta_{k}(t)\}_{k\in\mathbb{N}} is a sequence of independent one-dimensional standard Wiener processes.

However, to the best of our knowledge, this is the first work to investigate the finite-time extinction of SFDEs driven by general nonlinear multiplicative noise. Furthermore, in contrast to previous studies [5, 6, 7, 8], we establish finite-time extinction with probability one for arbitrary spatial dimensions (under the standard dimension-dependent range for rr).

Remark 3.7.

Beyond the aforementioned models, our results apply to all examples in [42, 57] under both linear and superlinear multiplicative noise perturbations; we omit the details for brevity.

4. Proof of main results

This section is devoted to the proofs of Theorems 2.4–2.6. Specifically, in Subsection 4.1, we construct the Galerkin approximation of SPDE (1.2) and derive uniform a priori estimates by employing suitable Lyapunov functions. In Subsection 4.2, we establish the tightness of the approximating sequence by leveraging a stopping time technique. Subsection 4.3 is concerned with the existence of weak solutions to (1.2), which we prove by combining the theory of pseudo-monotone operators, the stochastic compactness method, and Jakubowski’s generalization of the Skorokhod representation theorem. In Subsections 4.4 and 4.5, we show pathwise uniqueness and continuous dependence of solutions on the initial data (in probability) along with the Feller property of the associated Markov semigroup. Finally, in Subsection 4.6, we establish the finite-time extinction of solutions to (1.2) by utilizing a distinct Lyapunov function.

Set

Remark 4.1.

Here the intersection space 𝒵T1\mathcal{Z}^{1}_{T} takes the following intersection topology denoted by τ𝒵T1\tau_{\mathcal{Z}^{1}_{T}}: the class of open sets of 𝒵T1\mathcal{Z}^{1}_{T} are generated by the sets of the form 𝒪1∩𝒪2∩𝒪3\mathscr{O}_{1}\cap\mathscr{O}_{2}\cap\mathscr{O}_{3}, where 𝒪1\mathscr{O}_{1}, 𝒪2\mathscr{O}_{2} and 𝒪3\mathscr{O}_{3} are the open sets in ℂT​(𝕍∗)\mathbb{C}_{T}(\mathbb{V}^{*}), Lα​([0,T],ℍ)L^{\alpha}([0,T];\mathbb{H}) and Lwα​([0,T],𝕍)L^{\alpha}_{w}([0,T];\mathbb{V}), respectively. Let ℬ⁡(τ𝒵T1)\mathscr{B}(\tau_{\mathcal{Z}^{1}_{T}}) be the corresponding Borel σ\sigma-algebra.

In the following, we formulate the compactness criterion for the space 𝒵T1\mathcal{Z}^{1}_{T}.

Let 𝒦\mathcal{K} be a subset of 𝒵T1\mathcal{Z}^{1}_{T} such that the following conditions hold

Now, let {X(n)}n∈ℕ\{X^{(n)}\}_{n\in\mathbb{N}} denote a sequence in 𝒦\mathcal{K}. It is sufficient to prove that there exists an element X∈𝒦X\in\mathcal{K} such that along a subsequence still denoted by {X(n)}n∈ℕ\{X^{(n)}\}_{n\in\mathbb{N}}, we have

lim infn→∞∫0T‖Xt(n)‖𝕍α​𝑑t≥∫𝒩lim infn→∞‖Xt(n)‖𝕍α​𝑑t=∞,\liminf_{n\to\infty}\int_{0}^{T}\|X^{(n)}_{t}\|_{\mathbb{V}}^{\alpha}dt\geq\int_{\mathcal{N}}\liminf_{n\to\infty}\|X^{(n)}_{t}\|_{\mathbb{V}}^{\alpha}dt=\infty,

which contradicts condition (i).

Collecting (4.17) and (4.20), there exists a subsequence still denoted by {X(n)}n∈ℕ\{X^{(n)}\}_{n\in\mathbb{N}} and X∈ℂT​(𝕍∗)∩Lα​([0,T],𝕍)X\in\mathbb{C}_{T}(\mathbb{V}^{*})\cap L^{\alpha}([0,T];\mathbb{V}) such that

We recall the Aldous condition in the space 𝕍∗\mathbb{V}^{*}.

Definition 4.5.

A sequence {X(n)}n∈ℕ\{X^{(n)}\}_{n\in\mathbb{N}} is said to satisfy the Aldous condition in 𝕍∗\mathbb{V}^{*} iff for any ε,η>0\varepsilon,\eta>0, there exists δ>0\delta>0 such that for every stopping time sequence (ζn)n∈ℕ(\zeta_{n})_{n\in\mathbb{N}} with ζn≤T\zeta_{n}\leq T one has

supn∈ℕsup0≤Δ≤δℙ⁡(‖Xζn+Δ(n)−Xζn(n)‖𝕍∗≥η)≤ε.\sup_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\sup_{0\leq\Delta\leq\delta}\mathbb{P}(\|X^{(n)}_{\zeta_{n}+\Delta}-X^{(n)}_{\zeta_{n}}\|_{\mathbb{V}^{*}}\geq\eta)\leq\varepsilon.

The following lemma presents a tightness criterion for the laws of sequence {X(n)}n∈ℕ\{X^{(n)}\}_{n\in\mathbb{N}} on 𝒵T1\mathcal{Z}^{1}_{T}.

Lemma 4.6.

Let {X(n)}n∈ℕ\{X^{(n)}\}_{n\in\mathbb{N}} be a sequence of continuous {ℱt}\{\mathscr{F}_{t}\}-adapted 𝕍∗\mathbb{V}^{*}-valued processes such that

    limR→∞supn∈ℕℙ⁡(∫0T‖Xt(n)‖𝕍α​𝑑t>R)=0,\lim_{R\rightarrow\infty}\sup_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\mathbb{P}\Big(\int_{0}^{T}\|X^{(n)}_{t}\|_{\mathbb{V}}^{\alpha}dt>R\Big)=0,
  2. (ii)

    {X(n)}n∈ℕ\{X^{(n)}\}_{n\in\mathbb{N}} satisfies the Aldous condition in 𝕍∗\mathbb{V}^{*}.

Let μn\mu_{n} be the law of X(n)X^{(n)} on the Borel σ\sigma-algebra ℬ⁡(τ𝒵T1)\mathscr{B}(\tau_{\mathcal{Z}_{T}^{1}}). Then for every ε>0\varepsilon>0 there exists a compact subset 𝒦ε\mathcal{K}_{\varepsilon} of 𝒵T1\mathcal{Z}_{T}^{1} such that

supn∈ℕμn​(𝒦εc)≤ε.\sup_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\mu_{n}(\mathcal{K}_{\varepsilon}^{c})\leq\varepsilon.
Proof.

In view of (i), for any ε>0\varepsilon>0 there exists R>0R>0 such that

supn∈ℕℙ⁡(∫0T‖Xt(n)‖𝕍α​𝑑t>R)≤ε2.\sup_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\mathbb{P}\Big(\int_{0}^{T}\|X^{(n)}_{t}\|_{\mathbb{V}}^{\alpha}dt>R\Big)\leq\frac{\varepsilon}{2}.

We denote

𝒦:={X(n)∈𝒵T1:∫0T‖Xt(n)‖𝕍α​𝑑t≤R}.\mathcal{K}:=\Big\{X^{(n)}\in\mathcal{Z}_{T}^{1}:\int_{0}^{T}\|X^{(n)}_{t}\|_{\mathbb{V}}^{\alpha}dt\leq R\Big\}.

By Lemmas 3.6 and 3.8 in [12], in view of (ii) there exists a subset 𝒜ε⊂ℂT​(𝕍∗)\mathcal{A}_{\varepsilon}\subset\mathbb{C}_{T}(\mathbb{V}^{*}) such that

μn​(𝒜εc)≤ε2\mu_{n}(\mathcal{A}_{\varepsilon}^{c})\leq\frac{\varepsilon}{2}

and

limδ→0supX∈𝒜εsups,t∈[0,T],|t−s|≤δ‖Xt−Xs‖𝕍∗=0.\lim_{\delta\to 0}\sup_{X\in\mathcal{A}_{\varepsilon}}\sup_{s,t\in[0,T],|t-s|\leq\delta}\|X_{t}-X_{s}\|_{\mathbb{V}^{*}}=0.

Due to the compactness criterion presented in Lemma 4.4, we conclude that 𝒦ε\mathcal{K}_{\varepsilon} is a compact set in 𝒵T1\mathcal{Z}_{T}^{1}. The proof is complete. ∎

Based on Lemmas 4.2 and 4.6, in order to show the tightness of {X(n)}n∈ℕ\{X^{(n)}\}_{n\in\mathbb{N}} in 𝒵T1\mathcal{Z}^{1}_{T} it is sufficient to prove {X(n)}n∈ℕ\{X^{(n)}\}_{n\in\mathbb{N}} satisfies the Aldous condition in 𝕍∗\mathbb{V}^{*}, which is given as follows.

We now give the tightness of {X(n)}n∈ℕ\{X^{(n)}\}_{n\in\mathbb{N}} in 𝒵T1\mathcal{Z}^{1}_{T}.

Combining Lemmas 4.2, 4.6 and 4.7, the assertion follows. ∎

The following lemma shows the tightness of {𝒜(n)(⋅):=𝒜(⋅,X⋅(n))}n∈ℕ\{\mathcal{A}^{(n)}(\cdot):=\mathcal{A}(\cdot,X^{(n)}_{\cdot})\}_{n\in\mathbb{N}} in the space 𝒵T2\mathcal{Z}^{2}_{T}.

Proof.

The tightness of {𝒜(n)​(⋅)}n∈ℕ\{\mathcal{A}^{(n)}(\cdot)\}_{n\in\mathbb{N}} in 𝒵T2\mathcal{Z}^{2}_{T} follows directly from the Banach-Alaoglu theorem and the estimate (4.13). ∎

4.3. Passage to the limit

In this part, we aim to prove Theorems 2.4, where the Jakubowski’s beautiful generalization of the Skorokhod’s representation theorem, in the form presented by Brzeźniak and Ondreját, for nonmetric spaces (see Lemma 5.1 in Appendix) and the theory of pseudo-monotone operators play a crucial role.

In order to apply Jakubowski’s version of the Skorokhod theorem, we first verify that 𝒵T1\mathcal{Z}_{T}^{1} is a standard Borel space (see Appendix for the definition), whose proof is inspired by [38].

Lemma 4.10.

𝒵T1\mathcal{Z}_{T}^{1} is a standard Borel space.

Proof.

Let 𝒴:=L2​([0,T],𝕍∗)\mathcal{Y}:=L^{2}([0,T];\mathbb{V}^{*}) with Borel σ\sigma-algebra ℬ⁡(𝒴)\mathscr{B}(\mathcal{Y}). In order to show the assertion, according to Theorem 2.3 of Chapter V in [51] and the fact that 𝒴\mathcal{Y} is a standard Borel space, it is sufficient to show the following three claims:

(i) the embedding 𝒵T1⊂𝒴\mathcal{Z}_{T}^{1}\subset\mathcal{Y} is continuous;

(ii) 𝒵T1∈ℬ⁡(𝒴)\mathcal{Z}_{T}^{1}\in\mathscr{B}(\mathcal{Y});

(iii) ℬ⁡(τ𝒵T1)=ℬ⁡(𝒴)∩𝒵T1\mathscr{B}(\tau_{\mathcal{Z}^{1}_{T}})=\mathscr{B}(\mathcal{Y})\cap\mathcal{Z}^{1}_{T}.

First, the claim (i) follows directly from ℂT​(𝕍∗)⊂𝒴\mathbb{C}_{T}(\mathbb{V}^{*})\subset\mathcal{Y} continuously. Next, we focus on proving claims (ii) and (iii).

Proof of (ii). By claim (i) we have

(4.30) ℬ⁡(𝒴)∩𝒵T1⊂ℬ⁡(τ𝒵T1).\mathscr{B}(\mathcal{Y})\cap\mathcal{Z}^{1}_{T}\subset\mathscr{B}(\tau_{\mathcal{Z}^{1}_{T}}).

Fix N∈ℕN\in\mathbb{N}. Let us denote

(LNα​([0,T],𝕍))w:={x∈Lα​([0,T],𝕍)|‖x‖Lα​([0,T],𝕍)≤N},(L^{\alpha}_{N}([0,T];\mathbb{V}))_{w}:=\Big\{x\in L^{\alpha}([0,T];\mathbb{V})\big|\|x\|_{L^{\alpha}([0,T];\mathbb{V})}\leq N\Big\},

which is endowed with the weak topology on Lα​([0,T],𝕍)L^{\alpha}([0,T];\mathbb{V}). Then (LNα​([0,T],𝕍))w(L^{\alpha}_{N}([0,T];\mathbb{V}))_{w} is a compact and metrizable, hence complete and separable, space with metric d1d_{1}. Fix N∈ℕN\in\mathbb{N}. Set

𝒵T(N):=(LNα​([0,T],𝕍))w∩ℂT​(𝕍∗)∩Lα​([0,T],ℍ),\mathcal{Z}_{T}^{(N)}:=(L^{\alpha}_{N}([0,T];\mathbb{V}))_{w}\cap\mathbb{C}_{T}(\mathbb{V}^{*})\cap L^{\alpha}([0,T];\mathbb{H}),

which is a closed subset of 𝒵T1\mathcal{Z}^{1}_{T}. The metrics on ℂT​(𝕍∗)\mathbb{C}_{T}(\mathbb{V}^{*}) and Lα​([0,T],ℍ)L^{\alpha}([0,T];\mathbb{H}) are denoted by d2d_{2} and d3d_{3}, respectively. Now, let 𝒵T(N)\mathcal{Z}_{T}^{(N)} be endowed with the metric d:=max⁡{d1,d2,d3}d:=\max\{d_{1},d_{2},d_{3}\}. Since the intersection of finite separable metric space (with the maximal metric) is a separable metric space, it follows that 𝒵T(N)\mathcal{Z}_{T}^{(N)} is a separable metric space. We intend to show that 𝒵T(N)\mathcal{Z}_{T}^{(N)} is complete. To this end, it is sufficient to show that for a sequence {xk}k∈ℕ\{x_{k}\}_{k\in\mathbb{N}} converging to x(i)x^{(i)} in did_{i}, i=1,2,3i=1,2,3, we have

(4.31) x(1)=x(2)=x(3).x^{(1)}=x^{(2)}=x^{(3)}.

Since xk⇀x(1)x_{k}\rightharpoonup x^{(1)} and xk⇀x(3)x_{k}\rightharpoonup x^{(3)} both in Lα​([0,T],ℍ)L^{\alpha}([0,T];\mathbb{H}), it follows that

x(1)=x(3).x^{(1)}=x^{(3)}.

In addition, xk→x(2)x_{k}\to x^{(2)} and xk→x(3)x_{k}\to x^{(3)} both in Lα​([0,T],𝕍∗)L^{\alpha}([0,T];\mathbb{V}^{*}), we can deduce that

x(2)=x(3).x^{(2)}=x^{(3)}.

Hence, (4.31) follows, then 𝒵T(N)\mathcal{Z}_{T}^{(N)} is a complete separable metric space. Furthermore, the following embeddings are continuous

(4.32) (𝒵T(N),d)⊂(𝒵T1,τ𝒵T1)⊂𝒴.(\mathcal{Z}_{T}^{(N)},d)\subset(\mathcal{Z}^{1}_{T},\tau_{\mathcal{Z}^{1}_{T}})\subset\mathcal{Y}.

Therefore, in view of Theorem 2.4 of Chapter V in [51] we can obtain

(4.33) ℬ⁡((𝒵T(N),d))⊂ℬ⁡(𝒴).\mathscr{B}((\mathcal{Z}_{T}^{(N)},d))\subset\mathscr{B}(\mathcal{Y}).

Moreover, by (4.32) we have

(4.34) ℬ⁡(𝒴)∩𝒵T(N)⊂ℬ⁡((𝒵T(N),d)).\mathscr{B}(\mathcal{Y})\cap\mathcal{Z}_{T}^{(N)}\subset\mathscr{B}((\mathcal{Z}_{T}^{(N)},d)).

Combining (4.33)-(4.34) we obtain

(4.35) ℬ⁡((𝒵T(N),d))=ℬ⁡(𝒴)∩𝒵T(N),\mathscr{B}((\mathcal{Z}_{T}^{(N)},d))=\mathscr{B}(\mathcal{Y})\cap\mathcal{Z}_{T}^{(N)},

which yields that

𝒵T1=⋃N=1∞𝒵T(N)∈ℬ⁡(𝒴).\mathcal{Z}^{1}_{T}=\bigcup_{N=1}^{\infty}\mathcal{Z}_{T}^{(N)}\in\mathscr{B}(\mathcal{Y}).

The proof of claim (ii) is completed.

Proof of (iii). Since 𝒵T(N)\mathcal{Z}_{T}^{(N)} is the closed subset of 𝒵T1\mathcal{Z}_{T}^{1}, it is clear that 𝒵T(N)∈ℬ⁡(τ𝒵T1)\mathcal{Z}_{T}^{(N)}\in\mathscr{B}(\tau_{\mathcal{Z}^{1}_{T}}). Then we can obtain

ℬ⁡(τ𝒵T1)∩𝒵T(N)={B∈ℬ⁡(τ𝒵T1)|B⊂𝒵T(N)}\mathscr{B}(\tau_{\mathcal{Z}^{1}_{T}})\cap\mathcal{Z}_{T}^{(N)}=\Big\{B\in\mathscr{B}(\tau_{\mathcal{Z}^{1}_{T}})|B\subset\mathcal{Z}_{T}^{(N)}\Big\}

and

ℬ⁡(τ𝒵T1)=⋃N=1∞{B∈ℬ⁡(τ𝒵T1)|B⊂𝒵T(N)}.\mathscr{B}(\tau_{\mathcal{Z}^{1}_{T}})=\bigcup_{N=1}^{\infty}\Big\{B\in\mathscr{B}(\tau_{\mathcal{Z}^{1}_{T}})|B\subset\mathcal{Z}_{T}^{(N)}\Big\}.

Moreover, the embedding (𝒵T(N),d)⊂(𝒵T(N),τ𝒵T1∩𝒵T(N))(\mathcal{Z}_{T}^{(N)},d)\subset(\mathcal{Z}_{T}^{(N)},\tau_{\mathcal{Z}^{1}_{T}}\cap\mathcal{Z}_{T}^{(N)}) is continuous, which implies

(4.36) ℬ⁡(τ𝒵T1∩𝒵T(N))⊂ℬ⁡((𝒵T(N),d)).\mathscr{B}(\tau_{\mathcal{Z}^{1}_{T}}\cap\mathcal{Z}_{T}^{(N)})\subset\mathscr{B}((\mathcal{Z}_{T}^{(N)},d)).

Suppose that AA is an τ𝒵T1\tau_{\mathcal{Z}^{1}_{T}}-closed subset of 𝒵T1\mathcal{Z}^{1}_{T}. Then A∩𝒵T(N)A\cap\mathcal{Z}_{T}^{(N)} is τ𝒵T1\tau_{\mathcal{Z}^{1}_{T}}-closed. Then by (4.35) and (4.36) we have

A∩𝒵T(N)∈\displaystyle A\cap\mathcal{Z}_{T}^{(N)}\in\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\! ℬ⁡(τ𝒵T1∩𝒵T(N))\displaystyle\mathscr{B}(\tau_{\mathcal{Z}^{1}_{T}}\cap\mathcal{Z}_{T}^{(N)})
⊂\displaystyle\subset\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\! ℬ⁡((𝒵T(N),d))\displaystyle\mathscr{B}((\mathcal{Z}_{T}^{(N)},d))
(4.37) =\displaystyle=\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\! ℬ⁡(𝒴)∩𝒵T(N).\displaystyle\mathscr{B}(\mathcal{Y})\cap\mathcal{Z}_{T}^{(N)}.

Note that 𝒵T(N)∈ℬ⁡(𝒴)\mathcal{Z}_{T}^{(N)}\in\mathscr{B}(\mathcal{Y}), in view of claim (ii) we can get

ℬ⁡(𝒴)∩𝒵T(N)={B∈ℬ⁡(𝒴)|B⊂𝒵T(N)}⊂{B∈ℬ⁡(𝒴)|B⊂𝒵T1}=ℬ⁡(𝒴)∩𝒵T1.\mathscr{B}(\mathcal{Y})\cap\mathcal{Z}_{T}^{(N)}=\Big\{B\in\mathscr{B}(\mathcal{Y})|B\subset\mathcal{Z}_{T}^{(N)}\Big\}\subset\Big\{B\in\mathscr{B}(\mathcal{Y})|B\subset\mathcal{Z}^{1}_{T}\Big\}=\mathscr{B}(\mathcal{Y})\cap\mathcal{Z}^{1}_{T}.

Then by (4.37) we have

A=⋃N=1∞A∩𝒵T(N)∈ℬ⁡(𝒴)∩𝒵T1.A=\bigcup_{N=1}^{\infty}A\cap\mathcal{Z}_{T}^{(N)}\in\mathscr{B}(\mathcal{Y})\cap\mathcal{Z}^{1}_{T}.

Thus, ℬ⁡(τ𝒵T1)⊂ℬ⁡(𝒴)∩𝒵T1\mathscr{B}(\tau_{\mathcal{Z}^{1}_{T}})\subset\mathscr{B}(\mathcal{Y})\cap\mathcal{Z}^{1}_{T}, which together with (4.30) implies ℬ⁡(τ𝒵T1)=ℬ⁡(𝒴)∩𝒵T1\mathscr{B}(\tau_{\mathcal{Z}^{1}_{T}})=\mathscr{B}(\mathcal{Y})\cap\mathcal{Z}^{1}_{T}. The proof is completed. ∎

Now, we need to check that the spaces 𝒵T1\mathcal{Z}^{1}_{T}, 𝒵T2\mathcal{Z}^{2}_{T} satisfy the conditions in Lemma 5.1. In fact, since ℂT​(𝕍∗)\mathbb{C}_{T}(\mathbb{V}^{*}) and Lα​([0,T],ℍ)L^{\alpha}([0,T];\mathbb{H}) are separable Banach spaces, it is easy to see the conditions in Lemma 5.1 hold. Furthermore, for the space Lwα​([0,T],𝕍)L^{\alpha}_{w}([0,T];{\mathbb{V}}), it suffices to put

fm(u):=∫0T⟨vm(t),u(t)⟩𝕍𝕍∗dt∈ℝ,u∈Lwα([0,T];𝕍),m∈ℕ,f_{m}(u):=\int_{0}^{T}{}_{\mathbb{V}^{*}}\langle v_{m}(t),u(t)\rangle_{\mathbb{V}}dt\in\mathbb{R},\penalty\ u\in L^{\alpha}_{w}([0,T];{\mathbb{V}}),\penalty\ m\in\mathbb{N},

where {vm}m≥1\{v_{m}\}_{m\geq 1} is a dense subset of Lαα−1​([0,T],𝕍∗)L^{\frac{\alpha}{\alpha-1}}([0,T];{\mathbb{V}^{*}}). Since {vm}m≥1\{v_{m}\}_{m\geq 1} is dense in Lαα−1​([0,T],𝕍∗)L^{\frac{\alpha}{\alpha-1}}([0,T];{\mathbb{V}^{*}}), it separates points of Lα​([0,T],𝕍)L^{\alpha}([0,T];{\mathbb{V}}). Moreover, since (𝒵T1,ℬ⁡(τ𝒵T1))(\mathcal{Z}^{1}_{T},\mathscr{B}(\tau_{\mathcal{Z}^{1}_{T}})) is a standard Borel space (i.e. Lemma 4.10), the σ\sigma-algebra generated by the sequence of the above continuous functions, which separate the points in 𝒵T1\mathcal{Z}^{1}_{T}, is exactly ℬ⁡(τ𝒵T1)\mathscr{B}(\tau_{\mathcal{Z}^{1}_{T}}) by Theorem 5.4. Thus all the conditions in Lemma 5.1 are satisfied for 𝒵T1\mathcal{Z}^{1}_{T}. From the same reason, we deduce that the conditions in Lemma 5.1 also hold for 𝒵T2\mathcal{Z}^{2}_{T}.

Set

ΞT:=𝒵T1×𝒵T2×ℂT​(U1),\Xi_{T}:=\mathcal{Z}^{1}_{T}\times\mathcal{Z}^{2}_{T}\times\mathbb{C}_{T}(U_{1}),

where U1U_{1} is a Hilbert space such that the embedding U⊂U1U\subset U_{1} is Hilbert-Schmidt. Since {X(n)}n∈ℕ\{X^{(n)}\}_{n\in\mathbb{N}}, {𝒜(n)​(⋅)}n∈ℕ\{\mathcal{A}^{(n)}(\cdot)\}_{n\in\mathbb{N}} are tight in 𝒵T1\mathcal{Z}^{1}_{T}, 𝒵T2\mathcal{Z}^{2}_{T}, respectively, it is clear that {(X(n),𝒜(n)​(⋅),W)}n∈ℕ\{(X^{(n)},\mathcal{A}^{(n)}(\cdot),W)\}_{n\in\mathbb{N}} is also tight in ΞT\Xi_{T}. By the Jakubowski’s version of the Skorokhod theorem, there exists a probability space (Ω~,ℱ~,ℙ~)(\tilde{\Omega},\tilde{\mathscr{F}},\tilde{\mathbb{P}}), and on this space, ΞT\Xi_{T}-valued random variables

(X~(n),𝒜~(n)​(⋅),W~(n)),(X~,𝒜~​(⋅),W~)(\tilde{X}^{(n)},\tilde{\mathcal{A}}^{(n)}(\cdot),\tilde{W}^{(n)}),\penalty\ (\tilde{X},\tilde{\mathcal{A}}(\cdot),\tilde{W})

(here choosing a subsequence if necessary) such that

(i) the law of (X~(n),𝒜~(n)​(⋅),W~(n))(\tilde{X}^{(n)},\tilde{\mathcal{A}}^{(n)}(\cdot),\tilde{W}^{(n)}) under ℙ~\tilde{\mathbb{P}} is equivalent to the law of (X(n),𝒜(n)​(⋅),W)(X^{(n)},\mathcal{A}^{(n)}(\cdot),W) under ℙ\mathbb{P};

(ii) the following convergence hold

(4.38) X~(n)→X~​in​𝒵T1,ℙ~​-a.s.,as​n→∞,\displaystyle\tilde{X}^{(n)}\to\tilde{X}\penalty\ \text{in}\penalty\ \mathcal{Z}^{1}_{T},\penalty\ \penalty\ \tilde{\mathbb{P}}\text{-a.s.},\penalty\ \text{as}\penalty\ n\to\infty,
(4.39) 𝒜~(n)​(⋅)⇀𝒜~​(⋅)​in​Lαα−1​([0,T],𝕍∗),ℙ~​-a.s.,as​n→∞,\displaystyle\tilde{\mathcal{A}}^{(n)}(\cdot)\rightharpoonup\tilde{\mathcal{A}}(\cdot)\penalty\ \text{in}\penalty\ L^{\frac{\alpha}{\alpha-1}}([0,T];\mathbb{V}^{*}),\penalty\ \penalty\ \tilde{\mathbb{P}}\text{-a.s.},\penalty\ \text{as}\penalty\ n\to\infty,

where “⇀\rightharpoonup” stands for the weak convergence.

(iii) W~(n)→W~\tilde{W}^{(n)}\to\tilde{W} in ℂT​(U1)\mathbb{C}_{T}(U_{1}), ℙ~\tilde{\mathbb{P}}-a.s..

Let (ℱ~t(n))t∈[0,T](\tilde{\mathscr{F}}^{(n)}_{t})_{t\in[0,T]} be the filtration satisfying the usual conditions and generated by {X~s(n),W~s(n):s∈[0,t]}.\Big\{\tilde{X}^{(n)}_{s},\tilde{W}^{(n)}_{s}:s\in[0,t]\Big\}. We note that by the claim (i),

4.4. Proof of existence and uniqueness

We first prove the pathwise uniqueness of solutions to (1.2).

Proof of pathwise uniqueness. Let X,YX,Y be two solutions of (1.2) with same initial value x∈ℍx\in\mathbb{H}. Then, the difference process Z:=X−YZ:=X-Y solves the following equation

Zt=∫0t(𝒜⁡(s,Xs)−𝒜⁡(s,Ys))​𝑑s+∫0t(ℬ⁡(s,Xs)−ℬ⁡(s,Ys))​d​Ws,t∈[0,T].Z_{t}=\int_{0}^{t}\big(\mathcal{A}(s,X_{s})-\mathcal{A}(s,Y_{s})\big)ds+\int_{0}^{t}\big(\mathcal{B}(s,X_{s})-\mathcal{B}(s,Y_{s})\big)dW_{s},\penalty\ t\in[0,T].

Set

τMX:=inf{t∈[0,T]:‖Xt‖ℍ+∫0t‖Xs‖𝕍α​𝑑s≥M}∧T,M>0,\displaystyle\tau_{M}^{X}:=\inf\Bigg\{t\in[0,T]:\|X_{t}\|_{\mathbb{H}}+\int_{0}^{t}\|X_{s}\|_{\mathbb{V}}^{\alpha}ds\geq M\Bigg\}\wedge T,\penalty\ \penalty\ M>0,
τMY:=inf{t∈[0,T]:‖Yt‖ℍ+∫0t‖Ys‖𝕍α​𝑑s≥M}∧T,M>0.\displaystyle\tau_{M}^{Y}:=\inf\Bigg\{t\in[0,T]:\|Y_{t}\|_{\mathbb{H}}+\int_{0}^{t}\|Y_{s}\|_{\mathbb{V}}^{\alpha}ds\geq M\Bigg\}\wedge T,\penalty\ \penalty\ M>0.

It is clear that τMX,τMY\tau_{M}^{X},\tau_{M}^{Y} are stopping times and limM→∞τMX=T,limM→∞τMY=T,ℙ-a.s.\lim_{M\to\infty}\tau_{M}^{X}=T,\lim_{M\to\infty}\tau_{M}^{Y}=T,\penalty\ \mathbb{P}\text{-a.s.}.

Let τM:=τMX∧τMY\tau_{M}:=\tau_{M}^{X}\wedge\tau_{M}^{Y}. Applying Itô’s formula to ‖Zt‖ℍ2\|Z_{t}\|_{\mathbb{H}}^{2}, which follows from the same argument as (4.66), and by (𝐀𝟐)(\mathbf{A_{2}}) we derive

‖Zt‖ℍ2=\displaystyle\|Z_{t}\|_{\mathbb{H}}^{2}=\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\! ∫0t(2⟨𝒜(s,Xs)−𝒜(s,Ys),Zs⟩𝕍𝕍∗\displaystyle\int_{0}^{t}\Big(2{}_{\mathbb{V}^{*}}\langle\mathcal{A}(s,X_{s})-\mathcal{A}(s,Y_{s}),Z_{s}\rangle_{\mathbb{V}}
OPEN+‖ℬ⁡(s,Xs)−ℬ⁡(s,Ys)‖L2​(U,ℍ)2)​d​s\displaystyle+\|\mathcal{B}(s,X_{s})-\mathcal{B}(s,Y_{s})\|_{L_{2}(U,\mathbb{H})}^{2}\Big)ds
+2∫0t⟨(ℬ(s,Xs)−ℬ(s,Ys))dWs,Zs⟩ℍ\displaystyle+2\int_{0}^{t}\langle\big(\mathcal{B}(s,X_{s})-\mathcal{B}(s,Y_{s})\big)dW_{s},Z_{s}\rangle_{\mathbb{H}}
(4.71) ≤\displaystyle\leq\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\! C​∫0t(1+ρ⁡(Xs)+η⁡(Ys))​‖Zs‖ℍ2​𝑑s\displaystyle C\int_{0}^{t}(1+\rho(X_{s})+\eta(Y_{s}))\|Z_{s}\|_{\mathbb{H}}^{2}ds
+2∫0t⟨(ℬ(s,Xs)−ℬ(s,Ys))dWs,Zs⟩ℍ.\displaystyle+2\int_{0}^{t}\langle\big(\mathcal{B}(s,X_{s})-\mathcal{B}(s,Y_{s})\big)dW_{s},Z_{s}\rangle_{\mathbb{H}}.

Then, we have

𝔼​‖Zt∧τM‖ℍ2≤C​𝔼​∫0t∧τM(1+ρ⁡(Xs)+η⁡(Ys))​‖Zs‖ℍ2​𝑑s.\mathbb{E}\|Z_{t\wedge\tau_{M}}\|_{\mathbb{H}}^{2}\leq C\mathbb{E}\int_{0}^{t\wedge\tau_{M}}(1+\rho(X_{s})+\eta(Y_{s}))\|Z_{s}\|_{\mathbb{H}}^{2}ds.

𝔼​‖Zt∧τM‖ℍ2≤0,t∈[0,T],\mathbb{E}\|Z_{t\wedge\tau_{M}}\|_{\mathbb{H}}^{2}\leq 0,\penalty\ t\in[0,T],

which implies that

(4.72) 𝔼​‖Zt‖ℍ2≤lim infM→∞𝔼​‖Zt∧τM‖ℍ2≤0,t∈[0,T].\mathbb{E}\|Z_{t}\|_{\mathbb{H}}^{2}\leq\liminf_{M\to\infty}\mathbb{E}\|Z_{t\wedge\tau_{M}}\|_{\mathbb{H}}^{2}\leq 0,\penalty\ t\in[0,T].

Therefore, the pathwise uniqueness follows from (4.72) and the pathwise continuity in ℍ\mathbb{H}.

□\Box

Now we have all the ingredients to verify Theorem 2.4.

Proof of Theorem 2.4. By combining the results in Subsection 4.3 with the pathwise uniqueness established above, the unique existence of strong solutions to (1.2) is a direct consequence of the infinite-dimensional version of the Yamada-Watanabe theorem, where the estimates (2.6) and (2.7) follow from (4.43) and (4.44), respectively.

Finally, the Markov property follows from standard arguments, such as those in [42, Proposition 4.3.3], based on the established unique existence of solutions. This completes the proof. □\Box

4.5. Proof of Feller property

Set the stopping time

In the following, we first prove the continuous dependence on initial data in probability, and then we derive the Feller property of the transition semigroup.

∥Xt∥ℍ2−α+δ(c∗)α(1−α2)∫rt𝟏{∥Xs∥ℍ>0}ds≤∥Xr∥ℍ2−α+ℳr,t.\|X_{t}\|_{\mathbb{H}}^{2-\alpha}+\delta(c^{*})^{\alpha}(1-\frac{\alpha}{2})\int_{r}^{t}\mathbf{1}_{\{\|X_{s}\|_{\mathbb{H}}>0\}}ds\leq\|X_{r}\|_{\mathbb{H}}^{2-\alpha}+\mathcal{M}_{r,t}.

We complete the proof. ∎

Proof of Theorem 2.6. Step 1. first prove (2.12). For any 0≤r<t0\leq r<t, by (4.75) and (4.77) we deduce

(4.80) 𝔼⁡[‖Xt‖ℍ2−α|ℱr]≤‖Xr‖ℍ2−α+𝔼⁡[ℳr,t|ℱr]=‖Xr‖ℍ2−α,\mathbb{E}\big[\|X_{t}\|_{\mathbb{H}}^{2-\alpha}|\mathscr{F}_{r}\big]\leq\|X_{r}\|_{\mathbb{H}}^{2-\alpha}+\mathbb{E}\big[\mathcal{M}_{r,t}|\mathscr{F}_{r}\big]=\|X_{r}\|_{\mathbb{H}}^{2-\alpha},

𝔼​‖Xτ2‖ℍ2−α≤𝔼​‖Xτ1‖ℍ2−α.\mathbb{E}\|X_{\tau^{2}}\|_{\mathbb{H}}^{2-\alpha}\leq\mathbb{E}\|X_{\tau^{1}}\|_{\mathbb{H}}^{2-\alpha}.

Thus, it follows that for any t≥τet\geq\tau_{e}

‖Xt‖ℍ=0,ℙ​-a.s..\|X_{t}\|_{\mathbb{H}}=0,\penalty\ \mathbb{P}\text{-a.s.}.

Step 2. As for (2.13) and (2.14), we set r=0r=0 and take expectation on both sides of (4.77), by a standard localization argument we obtain that for all t≥0t\geq 0,

δ​(c∗)α​(1−α2)​∫0tℙ⁡(τe>s)​𝑑s≤‖x‖ℍ2−α.\delta(c^{*})^{\alpha}(1-\frac{\alpha}{2})\int_{0}^{t}\mathbb{P}(\tau_{e}>s)ds\leq\|x\|_{\mathbb{H}}^{2-\alpha}.

5. Appendix

The classical Skorokhod theorem can only be applied in metric space. In this work, we use the following Jakubowski’s version of the Skorokhod theorem in the form presented by Brzeźniak and Ondreját [13].

Lemma 5.1.

((Skorokhod Theorem)) Let 𝒴\mathcal{Y} be a topological space such that there exists a sequence of continuous functions fm:𝒴→ℝf_{m}:\mathcal{Y}\to\mathbb{R} that separates points of 𝒴\mathcal{Y}. Let us denote by 𝒮\mathscr{S} the σ\sigma-algebra generated by the maps fmf_{m}. Then

(i) every compact subset of 𝒴\mathcal{Y} is metrizable;

(ii) if (μm)(\mu_{m}) is tight sequence of probability measures on (𝒴,𝒮)(\mathcal{Y},\mathscr{S}), then there exists a subsequence denoted also by (m)(m), a probability space (Ω,ℱ,ℙ)(\Omega,\mathscr{F},\mathbb{P}) with 𝒴\mathcal{Y}-valued Borel measurable variables ξm\xi_{m}, ξ\xi such that μm\mu_{m} is the law of ξm\xi_{m} and ξm\xi_{m} converges to ξ\xi almost surely on Ω\Omega. Moreover, the law of ξ\xi is a Random measure.

We first recall the definitions of the countably generated Borel space and the standard Borel space in the sense of Parthasarathy (cf. [51, Chapter V, Definition 2.1 and 2.2]).

Definition 5.2.

(Countably generated Borel space) A Borel space (𝒳,ℬ)(\mathcal{X},\mathscr{B}) is said to be countably generated if there exists a denumerable class 𝒟⊂ℬ\mathcal{D}\subset\mathscr{B} such that 𝒟\mathcal{D} generates ℬ\mathscr{B}.

Definition 5.3.

(Standard Borel space) A countably generated Borel space (𝒳,ℬ)(\mathcal{X},\mathscr{B}) is called standard if there exists a Polish space 𝒴\mathcal{Y} such that the σ\sigma-algebras ℬ\mathscr{B} and 𝒴\mathcal{Y} are σ\sigma-isomorphic.

In order to apply Lemma 5.1, we recall the following result from [38].

Theorem 5.4.

(([38, Theorem B.4])) Let (𝒳,ℬ)(\mathcal{X},\mathscr{B}) be any standard Borel space. Suppose that {fm}m∈ℕ\{f_{m}\}_{m\in\mathbb{N}} is an ℬ\mathscr{B}-measurable sequence from 𝒳\mathcal{X} to ℝ\mathbb{R}, which separate the points of 𝒳\mathcal{X}. Denote by σ0​(𝒳)\sigma_{0}(\mathcal{X}) the σ\sigma-algebra generated by {fm}m∈ℕ\{f_{m}\}_{m\in\mathbb{N}}. Then σ0​(𝒳)=ℬ\sigma_{0}(\mathcal{X})=\mathscr{B}.
